text:
President Donald Trump has spent years criticizing wind turbines, calling them unsightly, expensive and harmful to wildlife while arguing they should be replaced by fossil fuels and other energy sources.

His opposition resurfaced Monday during remarks in the Oval Office, where he again criticized "windmills" while discussing Europe's economic challenges, continuing a theme that has become one of the most consistent features of his public rhetoric.

Trump's stance has evolved from a fight over an offshore wind farm near one of his Scottish golf courses into a broader campaign against wind energy, culminating in executive actions during his second term aimed at slowing new wind projects across the United States.

Read More on News

Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email for comment.

When Did Trump Start Criticizing Wind Turbines?

Trump's opposition to wind energy dates to the mid-2000s, when plans emerged for an offshore wind farm near Trump International Golf Links in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. He argued the turbines would spoil the coastal landscape, damage tourism and reduce the value of his golf resort.

Trump fought the project for years through public campaigns and legal challenges but ultimately lost, with Scottish courts allowing the development to proceed. Many observers have pointed to that dispute as the beginning of Trump's long-running criticism of wind power.

His criticism intensified during his 2016 presidential campaign, when he increasingly linked wind energy to broader attacks on climate policies and government support for renewable energy.

The president has argued they are "ugly," damage scenic landscapes and hurt tourism, while he also claimed they are inefficient, expensive to maintain and harmful to wildlife, particularly birds. More recently, he has increasingly framed wind power as part of what he sees as misguided climate and energy policies that disadvantage fossil fuels and raise energy costs.

Although Trump signed a 2009 open letter supporting action on climate change, his rhetoric shifted dramatically over the following decade as renewable energy became a more prominent political issue.

Trump's Wind Turbine Timeline

2006

Trump purchased land in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, where he developed Trump International Golf Links. Shortly afterward, he opposed plans for a nearby offshore wind farm, arguing the turbines would ruin the view and hurt tourism.

2011-2015

Trump spent years challenging the Scottish wind project through lawsuits and public campaigns. Despite those efforts, the wind farm was eventually approved and constructed.

2012

Trump began making increasingly frequent public attacks on wind power, criticizing the appearance, economics and environmental impact of turbines.

2015-2016

During his presidential campaign, Trump incorporated criticism of wind energy into his broader message supporting expanded oil, gas and coal production.

2017-2021

Throughout his first term, Trump repeatedly criticized wind turbines while his administration rolled back a number of climate and clean-energy initiatives.

2019

Trump drew widespread attention after claiming that noise from wind turbines could cause cancer—a statement rejected by medical experts and public health authorities.

2021-2024

Out of office, Trump continued attacking wind energy at rallies and campaign events, frequently calling turbines unreliable and expensive while pledging to reverse Biden administration renewable-energy policies if elected.

2025

Within days of returning to office, Trump signed executive actions aimed at pausing or slowing approvals for new offshore wind projects. His administration later expanded those efforts, drawing criticism from the renewable-energy industry and praise from fossil fuel advocates.

2026

Trump has continued to raise the issue during speeches, campaign-style appearances and Oval Office remarks, frequently citing wind turbines while discussing energy policy, inflation and Europe's economy.

How Has Trump Acted Against Wind Energy?

Trump's criticism has extended beyond rhetoric. Trump's views on wind energy now influence federal energy policy as well as political debate over climate change and renewable power.

During his first term, his administration prioritized expanding oil, gas and coal production while rolling back a number of environmental regulations and clean-energy initiatives. Although wind development continued during those years, Trump frequently questioned the value of federal support for renewable energy.

After returning to office in January 2025, Trump took more direct action against the wind industry. His administration moved to pause or slow approvals for new offshore wind projects, ordered reviews of existing permits and signaled that future wind-energy development would face greater federal scrutiny.

Supporters say the measures are intended to strengthen American energy independence by emphasizing reliable domestic fossil fuel production and reducing regulatory burdens. Critics, including renewable-energy companies and environmental groups, argue the policies threaten investment, delay major infrastructure projects and could slow the transition to lower-carbon sources of electricity.

How Many Wind Turbines Does the US Have?

One of Trump's harsher criticisms of wind power came earlier this year at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, when he said countries investing heavily in wind power were "losers."

“There are windmills all over Europe. There are windmills all over the place, and they are losers,” Trump said. “One thing I’ve noticed is that the more windmills a country has, the more money that country loses, and the worse that country is doing.”

The U.S. ranks second in the world in wind power capacity, trailing only China.

America has roughly 77,000 wind turbines, making wind power one of the largest sources of renewable electricity in the nation. The latest U.S. Wind Turbine Database, maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the American Clean Power Association, lists 77,379 turbines across 45 states, Guam and Puerto Rico.

Those turbines are spread across approximately 1,700 wind power projects and represent nearly 160 gigawatts of installed capacity. Texas has the largest number of wind turbines of any state, followed by other major wind-producing states across the Great Plains and Midwest.

Wind energy now supplies a significant share of U.S. electricity, with turbines contributing power to the grid in states ranging from Texas and Iowa to Oklahoma, Kansas and California.

Despite Trump's repeated criticism of wind turbines, the technology has become a major part of America's electricity infrastructure.

Trump's Wind Turbine Claims: Fact Check

Trump has repeatedly criticized wind turbines, arguing that they are harmful to wildlife, unreliable as an energy source and damaging to communities. Some of his most repeated claims have been challenged by scientists, public health experts and energy researchers.

Here are some of Trump’s claims and what the evidence shows.

Claim: 'They say the noise causes cancer'

Trump has repeatedly claimed that wind turbine noise can cause serious health problems. Speaking in 2019, he said, “They say the noise causes cancer.”

Fact check: No credible scientific evidence links wind turbines to cancer.

Public health experts have found no evidence that exposure to wind turbine noise causes cancer. While turbines can produce audible sound and low-frequency noise, research has focused primarily on possible issues such as annoyance, sleep disruption or stress for some people living very close to turbines—not cancer.

The American Cancer Society and other medical organizations have not identified wind turbine noise as a cancer risk factor.

Claim: They kill 'all the birds'

Trump has repeatedly criticized wind turbines by arguing they are especially harmful to birds. During the final presidential debate with Joe Biden in 2020, he said to the former president: "I know more about wind than you do. It's extremely expensive. Kills all the birds. It's very intermittent. Got a lot of problems."

Fact check: Wind turbines do kill birds, but experts say they are not the largest human-caused source of bird deaths.

Scientists acknowledge that wind turbines can cause bird deaths, particularly among certain species such as raptors and migratory birds. However, studies have found that other human-related causes—including collisions with buildings, vehicles, power lines and predation by domestic cats—kill far more birds annually.

Conservation groups say the impact of wind turbines depends heavily on location and design. Proper siting, monitoring and technology such as improved turbine designs can reduce risks to wildlife.

Claim: Wind turbines are 'ugly' and damage the environment

Trump has frequently criticized turbines for their appearance, often calling them "ugly," particularly offshore wind projects.

In June 2025, he told Fox News that wind turbines "Cover up a half a mountain" and "are ugly as hell." A day earlier, during a meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, he said he would not allow them to be built in the U.S. because "They're killing the beauty of our scenery, our valleys, our beautiful plains—I'm not talking about airplanes, I'm talking about beautiful plains. Beautiful areas in the United States, and you look up and you see windmills all over the place. It's a horrible thing."

Fact check: The visual impact is subjective, but environmental effects are more complex.

Wind turbines do change landscapes, and some communities have opposed projects because of concerns about views, tourism or local character. However, environmental researchers generally distinguish between visual impacts and broader environmental effects.

Unlike fossil fuel power plants, wind turbines do not burn fuel during operation and do not directly produce greenhouse gas emissions or air pollution while generating electricity.

Wind projects can have environmental impacts, including land use, effects on wildlife and the materials required for manufacturing, but experts say those impacts must be weighed against the environmental costs of fossil fuel energy production.

Claim: Wind energy is inefficient and unreliable

Trump has repeatedly argued that wind power does not work because turbines only generate electricity when the wind is blowing.

Speaking at the Shell Pennsylvania Petrochemical Complex in Monaca, Pennsylvania, in 2019, during his first term, Trump said, “When the wind stops blowing, it doesn’t make any difference, does it? Unlike those big windmills that destroy everybody’s property values, kill all the birds ... And then all of a sudden, it stops. The wind and the televisions go off."

Fact check: Wind power is variable, but energy experts say it is a reliable part of a modern electricity grid.

Wind generation does depend on weather conditions, meaning turbines do not produce electricity at maximum capacity at all times. However, energy experts say that does not make wind unusable or unreliable.

Grid operators manage changes in wind output through forecasting, geographic diversity, transmission networks, energy storage and combining wind with other sources of electricity.

The U.S. Department of Energy and National Renewable Energy Laboratory have found that wind energy can provide significant amounts of electricity while being integrated into a reliable grid.

Claim: Wind energy is too expensive

Trump has often argued that wind power is economically inefficient and depends on government support.

During a July 24 Oval Office news conference this year, Trump said about wind energy, "It's very expensive. It's probably the most expensive form of energy."

Fact check: Wind economics vary, but utility-scale wind has become one of the lowest-cost sources of new electricity generation in many regions.

The cost of wind projects depends on location, financing, transmission needs and policy incentives. While some projects require government support or face higher costs due to infrastructure challenges, energy analysts say technological improvements have significantly reduced the cost of wind power over time.

Critics of wind energy argue that subsidies distort the market and that intermittency creates additional costs. Supporters argue those costs are offset by fuel savings and reduced pollution.

Benefits of Wind Energy

Wind energy became one of the fastest-growing sources of electricity in the United States over the past two decades. Unlike coal and natural gas, wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel, meaning they produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions or air pollution during operation.

According to the Energy Department and other federal agencies, wind power can diversify the nation's energy mix, reduce dependence on imported fuels and create jobs in manufacturing, construction and maintenance. Offshore wind projects can also generate large amounts of electricity near densely populated coastal regions where demand is high.

Supporters argue that expanding wind generation helps reduce carbon emissions, improves long-term energy security and lowers electricity costs in some markets. However, they acknowledge that wind energy also presents challenges, including the need for transmission infrastructure, energy storage and backup generation when wind speeds are low.

Connected mobility platform Teletrac Navman has launched a new feature within its all-in-one fleet management platform TN360. The new Energy Hub is designed to provide businesses with a unified view of energy usage across mixed-energy fleets, combining data about EV charging with legacy fuel data in a single platform.

“As businesses continue to adopt mixed-energy fleets, managing energy usage across fleet management platforms, fuel card systems, and multiple charging sources, including home, depot and public networks, is becoming increasingly difficult,” the company explains.

Energy Hub gives managers real-time vehicle data, including battery state of charge (SoC) and estimated remaining range. Building on Teletrac Navman’s existing telematics platform, Energy Hub supports configurable alerts and exception-based reporting that can identify overcharging, unusual fuel transactions and inefficient charging behavior.

Energy Hub’s dashboard provides fleet-wide visibility into energy consumption, transaction volumes, cost per kilowatt-hour and overall spend. Fleet managers can analyze trends, monitor live charging status, track charging events, and locate public charging infrastructure.

“The challenge is no longer simply collecting information but bringing it together in a way that supports better operational decision-making,” said Teletrac Navman CEO Alain Samaha. “Energy Hub helps businesses reduce fragmentation and gain clearer insights into energy performance, bringing these data points together into one platform and enabling a more integrated, data-driven approach to fleet management.”

text:
Lithium-ion batteries have transformed energy storage, but their production process has long relied on liquid-based methods that are both time-consuming and resource-intensive. In a recent breakdown by Ziroth, the spotlight is on dry electrode coating, a solvent-free manufacturing technique that eliminates the need for liquid slurries and energy-intensive drying stages. This approach not only reduces production costs by an estimated 20-25% but also enables the creation of thicker cathodes, which can increase energy density. By addressing both cost and performance, dry electrode coating could significantly advance the accessibility and efficiency of technologies like electric vehicles and renewable energy systems.

Explore how this method is reshaping the global battery supply chain, from reducing reliance on traditional infrastructure to allowing localized production in regions like the U.S. and Europe. Gain insight into the technical challenges manufacturers face, such as optimizing polymer blends for scalability and learn how companies like Tesla are driving innovation in this space. Whether you’re interested in the mechanics of dry electrode technology or its implications for future energy solutions, this overview provides a clear look at the path forward for battery manufacturing.

The Importance of Reducing Battery Costs

Although lithium-ion batteries are more affordable than ever, further cost reductions are critical to accelerating the global shift to sustainable energy and transportation. Dry electrode coating has the potential to lower manufacturing costs by an additional 20-25%, making it a fantastic option for the industry. By eliminating the need for liquid slurries and energy-intensive drying ovens, this process significantly reduces production expenses. For consumers, this translates to more affordable electric vehicles, energy storage systems and other advanced technologies. Lower costs could also help bridge the gap between clean energy solutions and widespread adoption, making sustainable options more accessible to a broader audience.

The Mechanics of Dry Electrode Coating

Traditional lithium-ion battery production relies on liquid slurries to bind active materials, followed by lengthy drying processes that consume significant energy and time. Dry electrode coating replaces this method with a solvent-free approach. Using polymers like PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), electrode powders are bound into a cohesive, dry film without the need for liquid solvents. This eliminates the drying stage entirely, streamlining the manufacturing process and reducing energy consumption. The result is a more efficient, cost-effective and environmentally friendly production method that could reshape the battery industry.

Overcoming Technical Challenges

While dry electrode coating offers numerous advantages, scaling the technology for mass production presents several challenges. One major hurdle lies in the interaction between cathode materials and PTFE binders, which can sometimes compromise battery performance. To address this, manufacturers are experimenting with polymer blends, such as combining PTFE with PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride), to enhance chemical stability and performance. Additionally, roller-based techniques are being developed to improve scalability and ensure consistent quality during production. These innovations are essential for overcoming technical barriers and making dry electrode coating a viable solution for large-scale manufacturing.

Performance Enhancements and Energy Density

One of the most compelling benefits of dry electrode coating is its potential to improve battery performance. By avoiding binder migration, a common issue in traditional methods, this process enables the creation of thicker cathodes, which directly increases energy density. Higher energy density allows batteries to store more energy, resulting in longer-lasting electric vehicles, more efficient portable electronics and improved renewable energy storage systems. Furthermore, dry electrode coating is compatible with solid-state batteries, which require moisture-sensitive manufacturing environments. For consumers, this means access to next-generation batteries that are not only more powerful but also more reliable and durable.

Transforming the Global Battery Supply Chain

The adoption of dry electrode coating could have profound implications for the global battery supply chain. Traditional wet electrode processes require specialized infrastructure, much of which is concentrated in Asia. In contrast, dry electrode coating eliminates the need for such infrastructure, creating opportunities for regions like the U.S. and Europe to establish localized battery production facilities. This shift could reduce reliance on foreign supply chains, enhance energy security and foster greater independence in battery manufacturing. By decentralizing production, dry electrode technology has the potential to reshape the global manufacturing landscape and promote a more balanced distribution of resources.

The Future of Battery Manufacturing

Dry electrode coating represents a significant step forward in the evolution of battery technology. While challenges remain, ongoing research and development efforts are steadily addressing these obstacles, paving the way for broader adoption. Companies like Tesla are leading the charge, investing in the refinement and scalability of this innovative process. As dry electrode coating becomes more widespread, it is expected to play a pivotal role in both current lithium-ion batteries and emerging solid-state technologies. For consumers, this means a future where energy storage solutions are not only more affordable but also more sustainable and efficient, driving progress toward a cleaner, greener world.

text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency wants to remove public notice and public comments for state-level air quality permits, a significant change to the 1973 Clean Air Act. The change — which could occur in a few weeks — would take away a common form of public awareness for a new data center and public participation, speeding up the review process.

In a July 1 news release, the EPA called the current public participation rule “burdensome” and said removing public comments will “streamline” the process.

Dry cleaners, auto body shops and gas stations are typical applicants for a Clean Air Act “minor source” permit. Gas and diesel generators for data centers, especially in the past few years, have been a sustained newcomer to the permit application pool. These minor source permits are reviewed by state agencies, like the Georgia Environmental Protection Division, while “major source” permits for big power plants or large industry above the minor threshold are reviewed by the EPA (known as a Title V permit).

Critics of the EPA’s proposal, such as environmental lawyers, clean air advocates and data center opponents across the country and in Georgia, called this proposal “alarming”, “anti-democratic” and “bypassing community notices” in a July 22 EPA hearing considering the rule change.

“This proposal could allow pro-polluters to move forward with permitting new pollution sources while bypassing community notices and the current channels of communication,” Kiya Stanford, Georgia state organizer for Moms for Clean Air Force, said during the hearing. “This is especially alarming to me in Georgia with the rise of possible pollutant sources like AI data centers rapidly moving into communities throughout the state.”

More permits in two years than the previous 10

The Georgia EPD does not have a running list of data centers with air permits, and not all data centers have air permits, according to communications director Sara Lips. They are not tracked separately or categorized separately in a database, she wrote.

But Lips shared industry codes (SIC codes) to search for data center permits for “most but not all” in the state that have “minor source” site implementation plan permits.

According to an SIC search, 20 minor source permits have been approved for diesel generators at data centers in Georgia since January 2025. From 2014 to 2024, there were nearly the same number (17) of minor source data center permits.

Diesel generators are used for backup power when the grid can’t supply power during a storm or an outage and, in some cases, as a main power source while the developer waits to connect to the grid.

Finding out about a permit application is a critical way for watchdog groups and advocates to confirm a data center or polluting industries are coming to town, community organizers argue, because most people don’t search for air permits.

“Even current announcements don’t reach the residents who will be impacted directly,” Treva Gear the Georgia community organizer for North Carolina-based environmental justice advocate Dogwood Alliance, said during the July 22 EPA hearing. “It’s up to groups like mine to notify them. Once they know, they are always ready to speak up and speak out.

“The idea that the EPA is considering removing this 1973 requirement is alarming and anti-democratic. (It would make) it easier for polluting industries to move into communities under a cloud of secrecy is not the mandate of the EPA or state regulatory agencies.”

Gear has notified residents and reporters about biomass plants in southern Georgia, like the Altamaha Green Energy plant. That biomass plant’s minor source permit was approved in October 2025 and received 15 comments for or against the plant.

In Upson County, Rusty Blackston, a community activist against a Brightmark Plastic plant, thanked the Georgia EPD for allowing a public hearing in-person in Thomaston in May. Of the 29 people who spoke, only one was in favor of the plastic-recycling plant. The permit is being reviewed now. Blackston said the minor source permit review exemplifies a founding principle of this country.

“The public needs to have an input into this,” he said during the July 22 EPD hearing. “Damage to our environment is not acceptable, and we need to keep the process going to allow people to attend hearings, to submit comments and to be able to voice their opinions. If you take this away, you are infringing on our rights to freedom of speech.”

While public notice has been a way for watchdog groups to notify the community, public comment for data center permits hasn’t been popular until recently.

The permits issued between 2014-2024 had no public comments, according to the Ledger-Enquirer SIC list.

The first hyperscale data center project in Georgia, Project Excalibur, by QTS in Fayetteville, received a permit in 2023 and had no comments during the draft review.

In June, two projects out of the 20 found since 2025 had public comment participation: Project Pegasus in Troup County and Equinix xScale in Henry County.

Minor permits could have major implications

But starting in January 2025, the Sierra Club consistently commented on all 20 projects, saying: data center diesel generators would degrade air quality, battery storage should be considered rather than diesel generators, stricter emissions control technology should be considered, and a study about the cumulative impact on Georgia from all data centers should be conducted, given their unprecedented rise in development.

The Georgia EPD responded to the Sierra Club’s comments with consistent remarks. On air quality, they point to the facility’s Toxic Impact Analysis (TIA), showing pollutant levels below the state’s Allowable Ambient Concentrations (AACs). They do not dictate facility design, and battery tech isn’t a viable replacement for diesel backup. No federal rule requires more stringent technology, so EPD won’t mandate beyond the existing rule, and the cumulative study request has been “acknowledged,” and they are “monitoring” the growth.

The QTS Fayetteville project had 205 diesel generators approved in 2023. Project Pegasus had 180, in May, according to their air permits. Alone, these might not seem like a substantial amount, but that is why the Sierra Club has pushed for the review of a cumulative impact.

“The main reason why we’re so invested in this is the air pollution that comes out of these plants has real impacts in the air, even though it’s called minor source,” Isabella Ariza, a staff attorney for the Sierra Club, told the Ledger-Enquirer.

The Sierra Club analysis found adding together all approved minor source permits in Georgia are set to house more than 2,600 diesel generators, according to the Sierra Club’s analysis in a public comment submitted May 11. They could be more than two coal and gas plants worth of nitrous oxide emissions.

“These 24 data centers alone provide 5.2 gigawatts of backup power,” their letter says. “At a minimum, if we assume all 212 data centers in Georgia operate 100 diesel generators rated at 2,000 kW, the total backup power comes to 42.4 gigawatts. Georgia’s power sector had 39.7 gigawatts of net summer capacity online in 2024. There may now be enough diesel backup generators at Georgia’s data centers to power the state’s entire electric grid.”

Ariza, told the Ledger-Enquirer via email that, when clustered together, the data centers’ minor sources act as a major source, leaving folks with difficult decisions during the summer heat.

“If Georgia’s 212 data centers are each allowed 99-ton annual NOx emissions limits, they could emit roughly 21,000 tons of NOx per year, close to double the annual NOx emissions of Georgia’s coal plants, Plant Scherer and Plant Bowen,” Ariza wrote.

“During power outages in the summer, individuals who live near data centers will be without AC and will be faced with a decision of whether to open their windows and be exposed to unnecessarily high emissions from the data center’s diesel generators or else keep their windows shut and bear the brunt of the heat,” Ariza said via email.

Burden of proof or proof of burden?

The Ledger-Enquirer asked the EPA about the burdensome process that the state-level agencies are experiencing.

When asked specifically how much time it would save, they did not give a specific answer, only operational procedure and their reason for the change.

“The time required for any specific agency to review and respond to public comments varies across air agencies,” EPA spokesperson Carolyn Holran said via email. “The purpose of the proposed rule, per the best reading of the Clean Air Act is to provide state, local and Tribal permitting authorities with greater discretion to identify the requisite level of public participation that is appropriate in their minor NSR programs…it would put state and local agencies most familiar with local issues in the driver’s seat to determine whether, when, and for how long to provide opportunities for public participation for proposed new minor sources and modifications.”

Ariza said the Sierra Club, and other “allied organizations” have filed Freedom of Information Act requests for surveys and meetings about the burdensome process. The EPA has not responded, and rejected the Sierra Club’s request to expedite the process.

After comments are reviewed by the Aug 21 deadline, the EPA can act as soon as they want, Ariza said.

Lips explained where the EPD stands with the EPA decision and other means of communities being notified through other permits.

“EPD is determining whether the proposed rule changes would affect public participation requirements per the state regulations,” she said in an email to the Ledger-Enquirer. “Not all data centers require an air permit, and some data centers do require water withdrawal or wastewater permits. Those that require water from local governments do not require public notice. But if a new water permit is requested, public hearings will be held.”

In July, the EPD issued a stop-work order for a data center in Newton County because it was illegally constructing a data center. Activists in Covington say the public participation in these processes made this possible.

‘Pop-up power plant’ delayed because of public comment

In Newton County, the data center in Covington has been delayed thanks to public participation and comments from the group, said Sustainable Newton president and co-founder Maurice Carter. He told the EPA this story during the July 22 hearing in hopes of not letting this new proposed rule come to fruition.

The nonprofit organization with 50 members was concerned when they heard about the California-based Serverfarm data center being built in Covington last fall. The data center wanted to use on-site power because Georgia Power couldn’t yet supply this site, as it was an old warehouse that would be transformed into a data center, according to Carter.

VoltaGrid, a Texas-based power provider, permitted 33 gas generators to provide 90 megawatts of electricity “behind the meter,” Carter said. At the same time, Serverfarm applied for 37 diesel generators for backup power, all in one permit.

The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of Sustainable Newton, filed public comments challenging the technical aspects of the VoltaGrid permit in December.

“We raised and challenged (Georgia) EPD’s December decision to allow VoltaGrid and Serverfarm to apply for separate minor source permits rather than undergoing full review of their combined emissions from a co-located operation,” Carter said during the July 22 EPA hearing.

Georgia EPD published a draft permit in March. Sustainable Newton reiterated the same comments in the draft permit and noted the EPD proposed the two entities to separate sources, allowing both to escape more rigorous Title V permitting, Carter said. The “behind-the-meter” arrangement also violates state law, Carter told the Ledger-Enquirer.

“We again filed comments challenging that arrangement and also pointing out that under Georgia law, under the Georgia Territorial Electric Service Act, a business can’t sell electricity to another business unless one of those businesses is a regulated utility,” Carter told the Ledger-Enquirer. “So VoltaGrid could sell power to Georgia Power, or they could use it themselves, but they can’t sell it to Serverfarm. That’s not allowed.”

Despite this, VoltaGrid still constructed their generators, and Sustainable Newton took aerial photos resulted in EPD’s stop-work-order to VoltaGrid. Serverfarm has since received a permit, but they remain liable for penalties and further enforcement actions. VoltaGrid has not received a permit, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

“It’s very obvious,” Carter said. “If we had not been notified and invited to comment, then nothing we’ve done would have happened. This thing would probably have been operating back in March, you know, when they got the draft permit. Nonprofits like ours rely on a transparent review process, giving local communities an opportunity to hold polluters accountable. Without that, people suffer.”

text:
It feels like a long time ago now, but Georgia’s biggest energy story once centered on the construction of new nuclear power plants. In 2009, for the first time in more than three decades, the United States began building two new reactors, Vogtle 3 and Vogtle 4, in Waynesboro, Georgia. The road to becoming the nation’s largest generator of carbon‑free nuclear energy was bumpy. The project endured major setbacks, including the bankruptcy of the lead contractor, Westinghouse, cost overruns exceeding $35 billion, and a completion date delayed by 7 years.

Despite those challenges, Plant Vogtle is now one of three nuclear facilities in Southern Company’s energy portfolio. But another major issue is emerging for the utility giant: the rapid expansion of data centers.

Georgia Power, Southern Company’s largest subsidiary, doesn’t build data centers, but it is deeply invested in a current construction wave. Data centers house servers that require uninterrupted electricity, large volumes of water for cooling, and significant land for construction. Add to those concerns about oversight, regulation, environmental impact, lobbying pressure, and transparency, and the industry becomes a complex one to cover, says energy reporter Kristi Swartz.

“I remember last year when Georgia Power was talking about a big expansion of its power grid, with most of that going toward data centers,” she said. “A source told me we have to look at this as something much bigger now than Plant Vogtle because of the money on the table and the amount of electricity that’s going to be used.”

text:
The race to replace Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is heating up as the Aug. 18 primary quickly approaches with several candidates eyeing the governor's mansion. Seventeen names will appear on primary ballots for governor.

On the GOP side, the pool includes Lt. Gov. Jay Collins; former House Speaker Paul Renner; James Fishback and Trump-endorsed congressman Byron Donalds.

Donalds, a former member of the Legislature and three-term member in the U.S. House out of Naples, is the prohibitive favorite to win the nomination.

On Monday, "First Coast Connect" host Anne Schindler interviewed Donalds to ask why he should be the Sunshine State’s next chief executive.

This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

(0:41) You are leading in a number of metrics — money, polling. You’ve got an endorsement from our president. And, many are saying that this is your race to lose. It’s predicated on, in many ways, money and this Trump endorsement. So, let’s start a little bit with money. You have raised over $100 million so far, between your (political action committee) and your personal campaign fund. And, a lot of money has come from some very wealthy people — a lot of billionaires and a lot of folks with interests in artificial intelligence.

So, I want to ask you about the influence of money in politics.

First of all, one of the recent donations was this $10 million that came from billionaire Citadel (LLC) founder Ken Griffin. Do you believe that it is appropriate in politics for someone to be financing someone to the tune of such a large amount of money?

I think campaign financing is something that’s really more a matter of free speech. If somebody decides that they want to take their hard-earned money and donate it to a candidate because they believe that that candidate is going to support values or policies that they agree with, then, in our country, you’re free to do so.

I think a lot of times when people talk about is it responsible, or is it something that’s helpful to politics, I think it’s because there is a frustration out there that elected officials, by and large, are bought and paid for. Let me be very clear with the listeners, and frankly all Floridians, I’m not bought and paid for by anybody.

When I talk with prospective donors, or people who’ve supported my campaign, I’m not asking them what policies they want to see. I tell them about my vision and what I think is going to be critical for the future of Florida, for Florida to remain No. 1.

Everything from making sure that our children are getting a world-class K-12 education; to how we’re going to manage the growth in our state; to how we protect the beauty of Florida and make sure we have fresh water for the future of our state. Those are the issues I talk about.

And then, what happens is, you have people like Mr. Griffin who decide after doing their own due diligence, that they want to be supportive of my efforts. This is much more about having a value system that allows for Florida to continue to be the best state in America. And, I think, that the reason why we’ve been very successful in fundraising is because there are a lot of people who have come to Florida. They fled other states — like a New York, like an Illinois — in the case of Mr. Griffin, like a California. And, they do not want Florida to follow those models. And, so, in looking at this race for governor, they’ve made the decision on their own accord that I’m the candidate that’s going to be successful. I’m the candidate that’s going to keep Florida as the No. 1 state in all of America.

(3:28) I think the people who think that there’s a bought and paid for sense in politics, is because, typically, policy follows money. And, lawmakers tend to approve policies, or laws, that benefit their moneyed constituency perhaps more than those who are not active campaign donors. Certainly, they have the ear of the candidate and the lawmaker, or the executive, once in office.

So, why would you be different from that perception in the first place? What would separate you from what we understand as sort of a pattern in money and politics?

Well, that’s because my policies and my vision really hasn’t changed in 15 years when I first got into politics in the Tea Party Movement. Same person, haven’t changed. When I ran for Congress the first time in 2012, I raised $80,000. Half of that was an in-kind donation from a family that wanted to support me, and they let me use one of their offices that they owned as campaign headquarters.

We didn’t raise any money, but the same policies around border security, immigration policy, limited government, low-tax environment, low regulatory environment, those are the same policies that I support today. So, I think what’s changed is, yes, through my time in the Statehouse and my time in Congress, we’ve built a lot of support amongst Republican voters across the entire state. And, in some respects, around America.

You know, people have come to know me and understand that I am a conservative who’s been committed to these ideals for a very long time, and I’ve been consistent on these ideals. I think you have people who want to see Florida continue in the direction it’s going, and they’ve decided to make contributions to my efforts.

(5:08) So, when it comes to changing or evolving, some might say, on issues, I want to ask you, particularly, about AI data centers, because that’s been a huge issue. …

Have you followed, in some ways, the changing perspective? We know that as many as 70% of Americans oppose data centers near them. That’s more than historically, opposition to nuclear power plants, which is kind of extraordinary when you think about it relative to what we know is the threat of a potential nuclear meltdown versus a center that’s known to be a drain on resources and also noisy; but, perhaps, not a life-threatening-type situation.

So, it’s interesting you brought the corollary up about nuclear power plants because I know how people feel about this issue. I’ve been traveling the state nonstop. I’ve been in 61 of the 67 counties so far. I know how people feel about these, but here’s what I found when I went and did the research. What I found is: In Florida, we’re a regulated utility state.

Your utility bills cannot go up unless the Public Service Commission votes to increase utility rates. (It’s) very different from Virginia. When data centers were exploding in Virginia, they’re not a regulated utility state. And, so, what ended up happening is those came on the grid, they took away power and the utility bills went up for everybody else.

We’re a regulated state. No. 2, Gov. (Ron) DeSantis just signed into law Senate Bill 484. Under state law, right now, your utility bills, as a Floridian, cannot go up because of a hyperscale data center. That is state law. We are going to keep that law on the books.

When it comes to water consumption, the first generation of data centers, that’s the stuff that people are looking at on YouTube. Yeah, very concerning. All they were doing was sucking water out of the aquifer every, single, day and then dispensing that water back out into whatever basin that was available in those other states.

Gov. DeSantis put it into law. It’s law today. You have to get a consumptive use permit from the water management district in order to have access to that water, the same way people who bottle beverages in our state have to get a use permit, the same way communities (and) planned use developments have to get a permit, golf courses.

And, so, those are the things, those are the protections that are in law today.

(7:50) Both of those regulatory agencies, the Public Service Commission and the water management districts around the state, have, typically, been fairly friendly to applicants.

I mean the Public Service Commission has allowed rates that have been very controversial and opposed by ratepayers. The water management district has continued to permit large-scale consumptive use permits when we know that we’re in a water shortage, when we know that we don’t have a resource that is sufficient (for) the growth that’s projected. And, so, when you say that those regulatory agencies, I mean, certainly, they exist. But, are they empowered? Would they act to protect voters in these cases?

Absolutely. I live in Southwest Florida. I remember 12 years ago when we had blue-green algae blooms that were coming because of the projects that were not done around Lake Okeechobee and the Everglades restoration. It completely damaged Southwest Florida’s economy. I know firsthand that if you don’t have fresh water, you have nothing. So, we are going to to protect the water resources of the people of Florida.

Secondarily, we are not going to let your electric bill go up because of a data center.

If they get constructed, the data center company, they’ll have to pay for their utility usage and it’s not going to affect other people.

Today, in Florida we have 5 gigawatts of excess power on our electric grid, 5 gigawatts.

What that means is if you’re talking about a 1 gigawatt, hyperscale data center, the most that can be constructed in our state is five. Because, you would have to be able to access the free access power — the stuff that has not already been spoken for, essentially, when you’re dealing with the utilities.

We’re not going to let somebody come in and build a 10 gigawatt data center. You know why? Because, then, it would drive up utility costs on everybody else.

That’s what the law does. Those are the protections that I think are critical for Floridians. And, the last piece is proximity. I don’t want next to my house. Nobody wants one next to their house. There’s a reason why they can’t be more than a mile away from a residential neighborhood. That’s common sense. So, I think, when you look at the data and you look at the information, you say, OK, we can do that.

One last thing I’ll say on this. What people are seeing on YouTube are mostly first generation of these hyperscale data centers. The new designs are either completely air-cooled, nor requiring water, or they have a closed-loop system on site where they take initial water and, then, they recycle that water for their own purposes.

(10:25) Would you say that your view has evolved or changed as you’ve been hearing from constituents and voters on this issue?

Not so much that it’s changed, per se, but, it’s given me more time to do more of the research and more of the fact-finding, so that we have a constructive policy on how to manage this for the future of our state.

What I hear too often from other people on the campaign trail is we’re going to do moratoriums or we’re going to do bans. What that means is they haven’t sat down and done their homework. And, the governor has a responsibility to sit down, do the homework, actually get the facts and bring those findings to the people of Florida.

(24:37) I want to talk a little bit about climate change and how it’s impacting Florida in particular. (We ask) in part because we got a question from Matt in Arlington (Florida) on a couple of environmental topics.

We know that people in Florida really care about the environment. And, I think there was some strong evidence of that when this governor proposed some alterations to state parks, including adding lodging the size of luxury hotels, golf courses, pickleball courts. There was a large uprising about that. What commitment will you make to protecting Florida resources?

Would you provide money for the Emerald Trail here in Jacksonville? (It) has been more recently defunded by the presidential administration, who clawed back some money that had been given to the city (of Jacksonville) to develop this 30-mile multi-neighborhood connecting trail.

Well, first to state parks, we are going to protect state parks and state land. We are going to do that, especially the ones that are environmentally sensitive, those that are largely based on conservation areas. We want to make sure that we protect those, and we’re going to do that.

(25:48) What does that mean? Would you pledge not to develop them in the way this current governor proposed developing them, adding recreational features?

No. We’re not interested in developing that property. We think that property needs to be held pristine for the future conservation needs of the state going forward.

If you’re going to talk about what property the state does own, the state does own a lot of buildings and some other real estate — not stuff that’s in conservation areas — we’re going to evaluate those.

Some of those properties, the state, probably, shouldn’t even hold anymore because the state is expending funds to manage those properties. And, they have, in today’s version of the state, and moving forward, probably, little value there.

But, when it comes to things that are in conservation areas. We have no plans to develop those. We are not going to develop those. We are going to keep those pristine.

(26:35) When you talk about buildings, are you talking about privatizing functions within state parks like vendors, restaurants?

No, no, no, no, no, no, no. I’m talking about buildings that the state owns around the state of Florida. We want to do an evaluation of those buildings already constructed. What’s the highest and best use of those? If the occupancy or use of those buildings is frankly up to snuff. If not, then the state will probably look at disposing of some of those assets.

(27:00) In terms of funding for something like the Emerald Trail …?

The Emerald Trail, I have to study. I’m not sure about the project. That’s something that we want to take a closer look at before I can make a determination one way or the other.

(27:12):Property taxes, a big issue before the state, could mean enormous cuts for local governments and municipalities, as much as $5 billion in the first year. Some local counties here would be impacted, because they are known as fiscally constrained. That includes Putnam, Union, Clay, Baker. Clay and Baker could lose up to 30% of their revenues. This governor has proposed sort of an emergency fund setup to backfill some of that money. A lot of people say you’re going to inherit a mess if this passes with 60% of voter approval.

What are you going to do to manage the situation for these underfunded counties like our local ones?

Well, first thing, if it passes, what we are going to inherit is a property tax cut for hardworking people in our state at a time where affordability is a major issue, especially for our working families and our seniors on fixed income in our state. It’s a major issue.

No. 2, a lot of our counties, not all, but a lot of them, when property values were increasing the last seven years, they could have gone to a rollback rate to smooth out tax increases. They did not do that. They let their budgets increase very steadily, very handsomely.

They didn’t go to a rollback rate, because they didn’t look at the people who fund their budgets, the taxpayers, and say ‘You know what, we could let these budgets rise.’

But, especially the Biden economy, how terrible that was — the inflation brought to us by Joe Biden and Kamala Harris and the Democrats — they could have smoothed off the tax increases. They chose not to. And, what they were telling people was: We’re just going to leave the millage the same. We’re not raising taxes, even though property values shot up.

So, now we’re in this situation where the people of Florida need relief. So, that’s what we’re going to inherit. In terms of the budgets, and the fiscally constrained counties, all 29 of them, what we want to do is set up a funding formula for these counties if this passes. So, that way, they’re not having to hire lobbyists and send them to Tallahassee to, essentially, sing for their supper.

(29:08) What would that formula look like?

We’re going to have to construct that with revenue estimating and with the members of the Legislature. So that way, there’s a consistent funding model for those fiscally constrained counties. And, considering the amount of money we’re talking about, the high mark that I’ve seen is $350 (million) to $400 million a year.

I think that’s something that we can definitely accommodate in the state’s budget if the amendment passes. And, those are for the fiscally constrained counties.

If you were doing a grant program, then what happens, essentially, the governor gets to pick and choose who’s going to get what. And, I just don’t think that’s appropriate.

I think for those counties, you set a funding formula. That way, they can plan their budgets and plan accordingly for the future of their counties.

If the amendment doesn’t pass, we’re going to use the (Taxation) and Budget Reform Commission, which is going to get sat next year, to come back and do a top-to-bottom review of all taxes and fees in Florida with the goal of eliminating homestead property taxes once and for all. And, if we can’t get there, if you can’t get the money to work, then we want to provide serious relief for seniors on fixed income and working families in our state.

(32:31) I do want to get to (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) very briefly. We know that ICE enforcement has been a big issue. I’m curious about — you were expressing strong support for ICE in January. Since then, there have been a number of revelations about the enforcement that ICE — that included lethal enforcement — that the officers involved were lying about the force they were met with and the circumstance surrounding those fatal encounters. Has your perspective changed at all on ICE enforcement and how this has all rolled out?

No. The biggest problem is a couple. No. 1, in the state of Minnesota, you had elected officials in Minnesota who were working with people who had a desire to obstruct federal law enforcement from doing their duty. There’s a reason why you haven’t seen in Florida what’s occurred in Minnesota. Why?

Because our law enforcement has a responsibility to work with federal law enforcement, namely ICE. If you create and foment a situation, like what happened in Minnesota, where you essentially are egging on and creating an organized, highly funded, highly orchestrated protest to impede federal law enforcement, that’s when things go wrong.

text:
Hamburg/Münster – The expansion of wind energy in the United States continues despite political uncertainty under the Trump administration. At the federal level, construction halts and delayed permitting are slowing individual projects, while the market continues to grow across the country. Wind turbine manufacturers such as Nordex are benefiting from this trend with new major orders.

According to the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), the United States installed around 6,900 MW of new wind power capacity in 2025, the second-highest volume worldwide after China. Wind turbines generated around 464,000 GWh of electricity in the same year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). Combined with solar power, wind generation reached a record 17 percent share of total U.S. electricity generation.

Nordex Secures Three New Orders for 81 Turbines

According to the Nordex Group, the wind turbine manufacturer has secured three new orders in the United States with a combined capacity of more than 480 MW. The contracts cover the supply of 81 N163/5.X turbines. The company did not disclose the customers or project locations. The turbines will be manufactured at Nordex's plant in the U.S. state of Iowa.

"These new orders reflect once again the trust our customers place in Nordex and in our ability to deliver and service projects reliably and efficiently," said Manav Sharma, CEO of Nordex North America. He added that strong customer partnerships and robust manufacturing capabilities continued to drive positive momentum in the region.

Federal Permitting Halts, Growth at State Level

The Trump administration has issued executive orders halting construction at several offshore wind farms and, through the Pentagon, has also delayed permitting for around 165 onshore projects on private land. At the state level, however, expansion continues in states such as Texas, Oklahoma and Iowa: Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP) expect around 46,000 MW of new capacity to be added between 2025 and 2029, driven in part by rising electricity demand from data centers. Growth is being constrained by tariffs on turbine components and continued uncertainty around permitting procedures and federal energy policy.

With local manufacturing in Iowa, Nordex is positioning itself in a market environment in which states and utilities are driving wind energy expansion independently of federal policy. For turbine manufacturers, the U.S. onshore market therefore remains a key growth area despite political uncertainty at the federal level.

Nordex Share Price Rises

Nordex shares, listed on the RENIXX World, rose 1.96 percent to EUR 40.54 in trading on the Stuttgart Stock Exchange on August 4, 2026 (as of 2:16 p.m.). Compared with the closing price at year-end (EUR 29.18 on December 30, 2025), the share is up 38.9 percent.

text:
On Monday, in apparent response to concerns about potential disruption to the Texas electrical grid, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the state’s top two energy agencies to pause any new data center grid connections while the effect of those connections is studied by the state.

In a letter to the heads of the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the governor cited the 474 gigawatts of power under request for bulk-power projects, an amount more than five times the state’s record peak demand. About 90 percent of those projects are data centers, the governor noted.

“That unprecedented load growth could endanger the reliability and stability of the Texas electric grid,” wrote Abbott.

“Our top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life. That includes providing affordable energy, maintaining a reliable electric grid, preserving water for our communities, and championing Texas values. Those priorities can, and must, be achieved while also creating the jobs and providing the economic opportunity that comes with our national leadership in technological innovation and investment.”

Abbott said that the two agencies “must conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process before any additional data centers are approved to move forward.”

“Any project that fails to comply with requirements set forth by the PUC and ERCOT, and by state law, must be denied connection to the Texas grid.”

“The failure of some data centers to comply with the PUC’s survey measuring water and power usage under the General Appropriations Act makes this necessary.”

The letter asks the agencies to collect and assess each project’s construction and operational plans, including the extent to which they are developing on-site electrical generation and behind-the-meter power sourcing that might reduce their demands on the ERCOT grid.

In addition, the governor is also demanding financial and social information about the data projects, ranging from their reliance on tax incentives, abatements and other forms of public assistance to details about their ownership.

But alongside power consumption and interconnection issues, the letter also orders the agencies to obtain information from the various data center projects regarding their potential peak water usage and their impact on neighboring property owners, “including noise mitigation, light controls, setbacks, traffic improvements, emergency response coordination and other community protection measures…”

Most, but not all, of Texas lives in the ERCOT grid, independent of both NERC and FERC authority. The governor’s move comes at a time when industry and federal regulators are giving mixed signals about the threat of massive computational and data storage operations on the nation’s electrical reliability oversight.

In May, the North American Electrical Reliability Corporation issued a “Level 3 Alert” — its highest — requesting data and planning information from grid planners and operators concerning complications caused by data centers that can even trigger the smallest disruptions in the grid. The deadline for industry responses was today.

By contrast, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued a “show cause” order demanding that the same regional grid users and operators identify and justify, as a national priority, any rules and processes that might slow down integration of large-load power sources related to data center development into their grids. That deadline is Aug. 17.

The issue pits disaster planning against the perceived need for regulatory speed, but the threat is not theoretical.

Data centers — whether for data storage, crypto-mining or computations for artificial intelligence — demand massive amounts of uninterrupted and stable power for their highly specialized and sensitive hardware. When a data center senses a power disruption or a change in voltage, it is designed to automatically switch to backup power sources, triggering grid outages because of the sudden loss of load.

The recent NERC warning grew from an incident two years ago in Northern Virginia. On July 10, 2024, a lightning arrestor failed on a 230 kV transmission line there, resulting in a permanent fault that locked out the transmission line, triggering a series of “auto-reclosures” — automatic attempts to reset system circuit breakers and restore power to the line.

The incident lasted 82 seconds during which there were six successive system faults, the longest of which lasted 66 milliseconds. The system worked as designed and power was restored, but not before the affected area recorded a dramatic rise in frequency, a significant rise in voltage and a load reduction of up to 1,500 megawatts that lasted for several hours.

But the Level 3 Alert by NERC was issued because a previous lower-level warning was all but ignored by an industry for which the penalty for missed timelines can be calculated in billions.

In May, ERCOT reported that a reliability review of large-load users revealed four West Texas data centers seeking connection to the grid that failed its reliability testing. Reuters has reported that ERCOT has identified at least 26 incidents attributable to computational users abruptly disconnecting from the grid.

A former regulatory lawyer, who asked to be unnamed, said Texas is foreclosed from some benefits of being connected to the national grid, but it does benefit by having a more unified regulatory regime than other states.

“Texas is the beneficiary of having been its own master. They’re not subject to FERC’s general rate and transmission jurisdiction. They have the state commission (PUCT) in a direct line of sight over everything, and so they can coordinate all these things.”

“In other parts of the country, it’s really hard. There are so many different players in the room, and a lot of those players don’t have any legal authority to tell a load: ‘You can’t interconnect here, or you can interconnect this data center.’”

“I think that’s where the tension is showing up more crisply. Now Texas has its own problems. But in this space, at least, they are the beneficiaries of a unified regulatory construct.”

text:
The EV fast-charging network operated jointly by Pilot Company, General Motors and EVgo has surpassed 300 locations and 1,300 fast-charging stalls across 40 states. The companies say the network now reaches roughly 75% of the contiguous United States, covering more than 2.2 million square miles. That puts Pilot’s EV charging buildout past the halfway point of the target the three partners set in 2022 — up to 2,000 stalls at as many as 500 locations nationwide.

Highlights

More than 300 charging locations and 1,300 fast-charging stalls now operating across 40 states

Coverage spans approximately 75% of the contiguous United States, or more than 2.2 million square miles

Pilot reports a Plugshare score of 9.41 out of 10 as of July 2026

The partnership is more than halfway to its goal of up to 2,000 stalls at up to 500 locations

Where the Network Stands

Pilot, GM and EVgo have been building the collaborative fast-charging network since 2022. Pilot says EV drivers have rated the charging experience at 9.41 out of 10 on Plugshare as of July 2026.

“Pilot is making the most of all drivers’ miles by making long-distance EV travel more accessible and reliable than ever,” said Scott Hundley, director of light duty EV and infrastructure at Pilot. “Reaching more than 300 locations reflects our commitment to building a coast-to-coast charging network and delivering an exceptional travel experience that shows EV drivers they matter.”

What Drivers Find at the Sites

According to Pilot, amenities available to EV travelers at network locations include:

24/7 staffed sites that are well-lit, with free Wi-Fi and clean restrooms

On-site retail and restaurants, plus food, beverage and convenience options

Overhead canopies at several locations for weather protection

Pull-through stalls at several locations for drivers towing a trailer

Windshield washing supplies

“Crossing 300 Pilot and EVgo fast-charging locations is an important milestone because it gives EV drivers more of what they need most on the road: simple, convenient and dependable charging,” said William Hotchkiss, head of public charging at GM. “We’re helping build a charging ecosystem that gives customers more confidence to take longer trips and enjoy the journey.”

Which Road Trip Routes Does the Network Cover?

With stalls positioned along major interstate corridors, the companies point to several long-distance routes now served end to end:

San Antonio, Texas, to Jacksonville, Florida — across the South, through New Orleans and the Gulf Coast

Nashville, Tennessee, to Charleston, South Carolina — through Great Smoky Mountains National Park to the coast

Detroit, Michigan, to Tampa, Florida — south through Cincinnati, Lexington, Knoxville and Atlanta

White Sands National Park to Saguaro National Park — from near Las Cruces, New Mexico, to Tucson, Arizona

Halfway to the 2,000-Stall Target

The 300-location mark leaves the partnership more than halfway toward its full buildout goal, a target that dates to the 2022 launch of the collaboration.

“Drivers are choosing EVs for their summer travel plans, and access to convenient and reliable public charging empowers that choice,” said Dennis Kish, President of EVgo. “EVgo is committed to delivering a seamless charging experience, helping drivers travel with confidence and enjoy the freedom of the open road.”

Charging locations can be found through pilotcompany.com/ev-charging or the Pilot app.

title: The EV Battery Boom Is Now Destroying Automaker Capital - Environment+Energy Leader
description:
The first phase of the electric vehicle transition was defined by a race to secure battery capacity.
The battery restructuring behind the number included Stellantis's exit from NextStar Energy, its Canadian battery joint venture with LG Energy Solution.
It was one of the flagship battery plants announced during the first U.S. and Canadian EV manufacturing surge.
Battery Joint Ventures Are Losing Their Strategic Immunity Battery joint ventures initially solved several problems at once.
The industry is not moving from EV investment to no EV investment.
text:
The first phase of the electric vehicle transition was defined by a race to secure battery capacity. Automakers announced factories, formed joint ventures, committed to long-term supplier contracts, and designed vehicle programs around demand forecasts that assumed electric adoption would keep accelerating. The second phase is being defined by the cost of reversing those decisions.

Ford, General Motors, Stellantis, and Honda have now disclosed tens of billions of dollars in impairments, contract cancellations, program losses, and restructuring costs tied to electric vehicles and their supply chains. Several battery joint ventures have already been sold or dissolved. Multiple vehicle programs have been canceled before launch, in some cases months before their scheduled production start. And manufacturing assets that looked strategically indispensable only two or three years ago are now being valued at a fraction of what automakers originally paid for them.

The pattern suggests these losses reflect more than a short-term sales slowdown. It shows what happens when capital-intensive manufacturing capacity is built around a demand curve, regulatory structure, and product strategy that all change before the assets reach full utilization.

Automakers Are Paying to Unwind Capacity

Ford's reset established the scale of the exposure. The company disclosed an expected charge of approximately $19.5 billion as it canceled or reworked electric vehicle programs, shifted resources toward hybrids and lower-cost EVs, and reorganized parts of its battery manufacturing strategy. That figure blends several different kinds of losses, including EV asset write-downs, BlueOval SK restructuring costs, program cancellation costs, and future cash obligations. Only about $5.5 billion of the total is expected to actually affect cash. General Motors followed with approximately $6 billion in additional fourth-quarter charges connected to its EV manufacturing realignment. About $1.8 billion of that involved noncash impairments. The larger portion, approximately $4.2 billion, covered supplier settlements, contract cancellation fees, and other obligations with a cash impact. GM also warned that additional, though smaller, charges could emerge during 2026 as negotiations with its supply base continued.

That distinction matters. An impairment reduces the book value of an asset. A contract cancellation means the company still has to transfer cash, because a supplier invested, reserved capacity, or purchased materials based on production volumes the automaker no longer expects to need. The loss is therefore not contained inside an assembly plant. It moves through the cancellation clauses buried in long-term supplier and energy contracts, the same mechanism that has been reshaping corporate energy agreements this year.

Stellantis Put a Price on Overestimating Adoption

Stellantis disclosed approximately €22.2 billion in charges, citing weaker-than-expected EV demand, changing regulation, supply-chain restructuring, warranty provisions, quality costs, and workforce restructuring. Management acknowledged that its earlier adoption forecasts had proven too optimistic, but that was one factor among several rather than the sole driver of the total. The battery restructuring behind the number included Stellantis's exit from NextStar Energy, its Canadian battery joint venture with LG Energy Solution. Stellantis sold its 49% stake to LG for $100, effectively relinquishing its ownership for a nominal amount.

That exit is significant because NextStar was not an exploratory investment. It was one of the flagship battery plants announced during the first U.S. and Canadian EV manufacturing surge. Selling the stake for a token sum reflects a change in how automakers value direct control of battery supply once projected vehicle volumes no longer support the original capacity assumptions. The write-down does not mean Stellantis is abandoning electrification. It means the company is no longer willing to preserve every investment made under its earlier strategy simply because those investments once appeared necessary.

Honda's Losses Show the Risk Extends Beyond Factories

Honda's March reassessment pushed the same issue into vehicle development. The company canceled three EVs planned for North American production, the Honda 0 SUV, Honda 0 Saloon, and Acura RSX, saying that launching the vehicles under current demand conditions would likely produce additional long-term losses. Honda estimated that total losses tied to its electrification reassessment could reach ¥2.5 trillion, or roughly $15.7 billion, and acknowledged that concentrating resources on EV development had weakened its competitiveness elsewhere, particularly in Asian markets where newer manufacturers moved faster on software.

This is not just a stranded-factory problem. Capital destruction is also occurring in engineering programs, tooling, intellectual property, supplier commitments, and vehicles that will never reach a customer, a widening definition of stranded investment that has also shown up in corporate energy efficiency programs falling short of their targets this year.

Battery Joint Ventures Are Losing Their Strategic Immunity

Battery joint ventures initially solved several problems at once. They let automakers share factory costs, secure access to cell technology, qualify for regional incentives, and reduce dependence on imported batteries. But they also locked partners into shared assumptions about chemistry, factory location, vehicle volume, and timing. When those assumptions changed, the partnerships proved harder to unwind than an ordinary supplier contract.

GM sold its interest in the Lansing, Michigan, Ultium Cells facility to LG Energy Solution as part of its capacity reduction. Stellantis left NextStar entirely. Ford restructured its BlueOval SK partnership with SK On, bringing the venture's two Kentucky battery plants under full Ford ownership through a wholly owned subsidiary rather than continuing to share control. None of this means joint ventures themselves have failed as a structure. What has changed is how much automakers are willing to lock in: ownership arrangements are becoming more flexible, capital discipline is increasing, and automakers increasingly prefer optionality over the largest domestic footprint they can finance.

The Losses Are Repricing Future Factory Announcements

The most important consequence will not appear in the write-down totals. It will appear in the conditions attached to the next round of investment. Boards and finance teams are likely to ask for smaller initial manufacturing phases and more flexible production lines, so a plant can scale toward real demand rather than a forecast. Contract terms are shifting alongside that: firmer vehicle-volume commitments, supplier agreements with lower cancellation exposure, and flexibility across battery chemistries instead of a single locked-in cell design. Some of that flexibility means building in a clearer path to hybrid or energy-storage production if EV volumes don't materialize on schedule, with tighter return thresholds required before anyone signs off on the next expansion. Honda has already said it will impose stricter investment caps and monitor post-investment earnings more closely.

That is the real transition underway. The industry is not moving from EV investment to no EV investment. It is moving from capacity-first investment to return-first investment, part of a broader recalibration toward return-first capital planning across the wider energy and industrial economy this summer. For battery suppliers, construction firms, states, and communities competing for new plants, that change reduces the value of an announcement that isn't backed by firm production economics. A multibillion-dollar factory commitment no longer guarantees that every planned line will be completed, operated at scale, or remain under the ownership structure originally announced.
