text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

As the all-important midterm elections draw closer, Democrats are fine-tuning their economic messaging while Republicans are…well, panicking. That doesn’t mean the 2026 mid-term results are a foregone conclusion, though. If economic messaging is all the Democrats to offer, they are missing an opportunity to motivate a key demographic, namely, voters who recognize that Congress must pick up the climate action ball dropped by US President Donald Trump.

Spokane Is Burning

The latest news on the climate front indicates that the global warming chickens have come home to roost, with a vengeance. On top of a series of record setting heat waves across the country, smoke from Canadian wildfires engulfed much of the US Northeast last week, and this week Mother Nature has followed up with three wildfires burning their way through Spokane County, Washington. So far they have consumed more than 600 buildings, many located within the borders of the City of Spokane. Thousands have been forced to evacuate, with some under urgent “leave now” and “last notice” warnings.

Meanwhile, the impact of wildfire smoke on human health is coming into sharper focus. Too bad US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has chosen this moment to launch a cooking show on teevee (roadkill, much?) instead of employing his media amplifier in the service of CDC health advisories, but such is the world we live in today.

Fortunately, the information gap has been filled by science. In addition to an ongoing advisory remaining on the CDC website, the journal Frontiers in Environmental Health has just published a research paper showing that an increase in wildfire smoke over the past 16 years has offset the public health gains of reducing pollution from transportation and industry. The new study pinpoints low birthweight and pre-term births among the rise in negative health outcomes related to the impact of wildfire smoke on pregnant women.

“Even in regions that are not strongly associated with wildfire, such as the southeast region of the U.S., wildfire pollution rates grew substantially during that time period,” summarizes the news organization Stateline.

What’s With All The Climate-Hushing?

In a nutshell, wildfire smoke is now the single leading pollutant impacting pregnant women in the US, on top of the direct, destructive impact of wildfires on homes, businesses, and communities. Moreover, wildfire hazards are just one of many climate-related impacts to hit the domestic electorate over the head on an up-close-and-personal basis beyond the oft-cited sea level rise metric, including increasing cycles of heat waves, drought, and flooding. Regardless of how far or near they are to a seacoast, more US voters are getting to know climate change on a painfully intimate level.

Clearly, if climate change is not the primary economic issue of all time, it is among other major economic issues left unaddressed (to put it kindly) by the current Republican majority in Washington, on up to and including the impact of the Iran war on fuel prices.

Nevertheless, word on the street is that Democratic strategists are encouraging candidates to avoid talking about climate change. A research team at the University of California – Santa Barbara, for example, cites multiple advisory groups and pundits that have advised against including climate change in campaign messaging.

“Candidates have listened: an Inside Climate News analysis of press releases from congressional Democrats finds that mentions of climate change have dropped 80 percent since 2021,” the researchers note.

Why Not Talk About Climate Change?

Rather than dwell on the situation as-is, the USC researchers took it upon themselves to investigate whether or not climate-hushing is sound advice for Democratic candidates this year. They summarize the climate-hushing argument in three parts:

Claim 1 Climate is not a top issue Voters care more about costs, health care, jobs and other issues.

Claim 2 The phrase “climate change” is polarizing The same policies labeled with climate will divide people along partisan lines.

Claim 3 Emphasizing climate change loses votes This does NOT necessarily follow from Claim 2.

In support of the climate-hushing argument, the USC team found that Claim 1 is true. Climate clawed itself up only as far as the #12 spot out of 15 in an exercise designed to test voter priorities, and there it sat. Meanwhile, the top three priorities, predictably, were the cost of living, the economy, and health care.

If you spotted the missed opportunity, there it is. To the extent that climate solutions address the cost of living, the general economy, and public health, climate action should be part and parcel of economic messaging.

More to the point, the study contradicts Claim 2. “Saying the word climate does not polarize. Identical policies drew the same support when framed as climate versus energy or clean air. Voters care more about the policy mechanism than the policy’s goal,” the USC team summarized, indicating that it’s important to provide a context and solutions rather than simply bandying “climate change” about.

A similar finding applies to Claim 3. “Climate supporters are far more motivated to vote on climate than climate opponents. Emphasizing climate actually increased support for candidates rather than lowering it,” the researchers explained.

For the record, the USC researchers tested each of the three claims through two national surveys totaling approximately 3,500 adults this past summer.

Now What?

It remains to be seen where the Democrats go with climate messaging as the 2026 election cycle heats up, so to speak. If anything, climate action provides candidates with a common-ground argument and a solid track record of recent support to pull on, considering the ambitious programs set in motion by the Biden administration.

That kind of universal messaging is sorely needed at a time when divide-and-conquer forces are working against a Democratic landslide, particularly in regards to Israel’s role in the Iran war. In addition, Democrats in office are not immune to criticism over broad structural issues that predate Trump, including the cost of housing, health insurance, and education alongside more recent developments like the data center boom and the rising impact of AI-enabled systems.

Digging into the particulars of the USC study, while 50% of those surveyed ranked “cost of living” among their top three priorities, a relatively healthy 14% gave a top three ranking to “energy and electricity.” The category “clean air and water” also earned 14%, while “climate change” clocked in at 12% — a relatively small showing but still worth a mention in campaign materials. USC emphasizes that caring about an issue is not the same as voting on it, but the team’s findings on Claim 2 indicate that climate-carers are significantly more motivated to vote for candidates who center climate change.

“Climate supporters and opponents were sharply mismatched. Supporters rated the pull of climate on their vote at nearly 75 out of 100,” the USC team reported.

“Opponents rated it as under 38 out of 100, a gap of 37 points. Clean energy followed a similar pattern, with a 36 point gap. These findings suggest that supporters will reward climate candidates, while climate opponents will remain relatively indifferent,” they elaborated.

Notably, the researchers also found broad, non-partisan support for specific decarbonization technologies, with rooftop solar taking the lead at 69% favorable compared to just 20% unfavorable. The team also cites onshore wind, large solar farms, and heat pumps among those with wide favorability margins.

“These findings suggest that climate messaging can be grounded in clean technologies themselves, which are broadly popular with voters,” they emphasized.

Readers, if you are voting this year, drop a note in the discussion thread and share your priorities. Better yet, find your representatives in Congress and let them know what you think.

title: 9 States With The Most Solar Panels (And How They Use Them) - BGR

text:
Solar energy is a key pillar not only within the world of renewable energy, but also in the total energy mix of the world. Interest in photovoltaic panel technology continues to grow as individual home solar installations are able to reduce the strain on grids and save individual residents significant money. Countries like China are steaming ahead with a solar power surplus the U.S. could only dream of, but don't make the mistake of thinking America is sitting on its laurels and letting the sunshine go to waste.

That said, making the shift to solar isn't easy, whether you're an individual or a government entity. It requires expensive infrastructure and careful planning. At a state level, the amount of progress toward making solar a key part of the energy mix has gone better in some places than others. Sometimes it's just that a state's geography doesn't mesh well with solar, but more often than not it's the exact mix of public policy and private appetite for this rapidly developing technology that determines how fast the rollout can happen.

So, which states are doing the best job of making the move to solar? We looked up the data from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) to determine which states are generating the most total solar power as of June 2026, and then we found examples of how each state is using its solar energy.

It should be no surprise that sunny and progressive California sits atop this list. Not only does it have the right climate for solar panels, but California has a long history of environmentalism and its support for renewable energy has been nothing short of exemplary. The state has an RPS (Renewable Portfolio Standard) that requires 60% of power to be from renewable sources by 2030. State net metering (where you offset your grid use with solar) is layered on top of federal investment tax credits (ITC) making solar highly attractive to both businesses and household.

The actual numbers are staggering. California has 55,510 MW of installed capacity, and it can store over 60,000 MWh of power. That's enough power to run 16,271,789 homes according to SEIA. Net Energy Metering (NEM) has helped homeowners save money on their monthly bills and reduced California's reliance on "dirty" power sources such as coal.

There's also the Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP), which brings a bundle of incentives to encourage the installation of solar infrastructure and to support existing installations. The potential savings are substantial, with the expected savings over 25 years ranging from $40,000 to $80,000. California's new energy experiment, called "Project Nexus," started in 2025 and uses solar panels over canals to both harvest solar energy, and reduce water losses from evaporation. California is also home to the largest solar farm in America, so this victory is unsurprising.

It's rare for California and Texas to be right next to each other on a list, but while each state has its own distinct character and culture, they share an abundance of sunshine. It's even more jarring to see that Texas is second on the list of top solar states, because it's also the top oil-producing state in the U.S. You'll still see plenty of oil pumpjacks throughout the state, but as Texas increases its focus on renewable green energy, you'll also be seeing more solar farms get built.

With 53,568 MW of solar installed, Texas isn't far from the top spot, but its storage capacity of 29,163 MWh is only about half of what The Golden State has. This makes sense given that unlike California, most of Texas' solar generation goes towards utility-scale generation rather than residential. Less than 2% of the rooftop solar potential in the state has been exploited so far, but despite this Texas still ranks third in the U.S for residential solar generation. In late 2025 solar output overtook coal in Texas, so there's no doubt that this oil-rich state has a bright renewable future.

An interesting thing to watch about this trend involves the number of tech companies that are moving from California to Texas, and it seems a data center boom is following in the wake of this shift. For example, TotalEnergies is set to provide a full Gigawatt of solar power to Google Data centers in Texas.

Florida holds a respectable third place in the national solar race, but despite being The Sunshine State, it sits quite far behind California and Texas in terms of installed capacity with 21,968 MW. Likewise, the state's storage capacity is virtually non-existent, with just 1,476 MW of room for surplus energy. Similar to Texas, Florida's solar industry is driven more by utility-scale infrastructure than residential.

Florida is sunny, but it is also notorious for its violent weather events, which is why it needs houses that survive category 5 hurricanes. The same weather that would be ideal for renewable energy sources such as wind and solar, also make things difficult. Residential rooftop solar installations, for example, are an issue since a storm powerful enough to blow the roof itself off will obviously also destroy any solar panels attached to it. Even so, Floridians are clearly pushing for rooftop solar with around 4% of homes using solar as of 2025, but experts expect rapid growth in the coming years.

One of the most interesting applications of solar energy in Florida is the production of hydrogen. This abundant chemical is an excellent energy carrier, and Florida has unique hybrid solar farms that use a portion of the solar energy to split water into oxygen and hydrogen. That hydrogen can then later be used after the sun goes down, bypassing the cost and environmental issues of chemical battery storage. The end result is just the same water that you split in the first place.

Given that Arizona is mostly arid and semi-arid containing no fewer than four major deserts within its borders, it's perhaps no surprise that it's rated this high in the U.S. rankings for solar power infrastructure. As of 2025, however, the state has only 11,751 MW of installed solar capacity, but what is surprising is that its storage capacity, at 20,245 MWh, is practically double that figure.

Like Florida, Arizona is one of the sunniest states in the country, so it has incredible growth potential. Especially with all that desert terrain. That said, we've already seen how solar farms in a Chinese desert can alter the ecosystem. By intercepting solar energy, the soil retains more moisture and becomes more fertile. This sounds like a good thing, but any ecological change can have unforeseen consequences, which means Arizona will have to think carefully on how best to use that sunny desert land. Arizona wants to be carbon neutral by 2050, though, so the pressure to find solutions is definitely on.

Arizona is already innovating with solar and nature by placing solar panels over crops. This practice is known as agrivoltaics, which generates clean energy while shielding crops and farmers from harsh sunlight. Doing so allows farmers to use the same piece of land for two purposes simultaneously.

While North Carolina has 10,093 MW of installed solar capacity, its storage capacity of under 1,000 MWh means that not much of that solar power can be stored. Not to be deterred, NC is one of the national leaders in utility-scale solar development, and as solar grows in this state, expect to see North Carolina's rankings rise when it comes to both its solar capacity and storage capacity.

North Carolina is known for having diverse landscapes within its border, and this is also a state that has a massive agricultural industry. While solar and agriculture have been growing together, utility-scale solar projects have taken up surprisingly little agricultural land. Where there has been overlap, NC has engaged in agrivoltaics similar to what we saw in Arizona. The state that gave us Pepsi, Krispy Kreme, and unique barbecue might one day mainly be known for its clean energy.

Given the diverse landscape, it makes sense that solar projects are equally eclectic. The U.S. Army stationed at Fort Bragg boasts the largest floating solar array in the Southeast. Producing 1.1 MW of energy with a 2MWh storage system. In 2024 the EPA granted $156M to an organization called EnergizeNC. A coalition aimed at giving solar power access to as many residents as possible by expanding rooftop solar, multifamily solar, and community solar for low-income communities in particular. NC's legislation is particularly community solar friendly, which means projects like this will steadily increase both solar capacity and equitable solar access.

At 8,290 MW of installed solar capacity, Illinois manages sixth position nationally. A much more pressing issue is the lack of storage capacity in light of all that generation capacity. The state relies on coal and nuclear power for baseload, which needs to change in the long term. Right now, Illinois can only store 93MWh of renewable energy. However, if new laws that have been signed by the governor take effect, then Illinois plans to install 3GW of battery storage by 2030. Given that this capacity is effectively nothing at the moment, this would be a tremendous achievement.

Clean energy is growing at a tremendous pace, and the state is focused on expanding solar deployment wherever it can. The Illinois Solar For All program is worth mentioning here, since it aims to help "income-eligible" homeowners and even people who rent access cheaper solar power. According to the program, the average annual savings on power for families that have been assisted by the program is over $1,000.

Another highly-notable project is Illinois Shines, a state-administered project that can award incentives to a wide variety of solar projects. This means that, like North Carolina, the spread of solar generation projects are diverse. The incentives given to solar vendors through this program can be passed on as savings to end users, which means it has the potential to bring more users into the solar fold. Illinois Shines is also actively helping public schools switch to solar, which has economic and educational benefits.

Nevada hits the seventh spot with 8,244 MW of installed solar capacity and 6,331 MWh of storage capacity. This is another state with open desert regions and a sunny, dry climate, making it ideal for solar power development in the future. While it might only be in seventh place for capacity, Nevada gets 33.5% of its power from solar — putting it behind only California for this statistic. This means that a third of those bright lights Las Vegas is famous for get their power from solar.

Nevada's Renewable Portfolio Standard was established all the way back in 1997 and currently stipulates that the state must get 50% of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Given that more than a third of its power already comes from solar and there's plenty of room to grow, this is a target that it might actually, realistically hit. With a current storage capacity that is so low, Nevada might be the best place to be over the next few years if you're a battery salesman.

In a wonderful nominative coincidence, Nevada's Freedom Park received a 1,500-panel 480KW solar parking bay system in 2024. This is a great example of solar technology pulling double-duty. shading parked cars from the harsh Nevada sun, while also turning energy that would have been wasted cooking a car into energy that can, instead, cook your dinner.

The Empire State is ranked eighth for solar capacity with 8,226 MW installed, but it also has a low relative storage capacity at 1,096 MWh. Solar only makes up a modest 7.7% of the New York's total energy mix, but it is growing. The NY-Sun program is aiming to grow that number by offering both on-site and community solar access and making citizens aware of the various incentives and tax breaks afforded to those who go solar in NY.

As for New York City, the drive for rooftop solar is substantial. NY-Sun is providing $200M of funding to add a gigawatt of power generation to the state as a whole from rooftop and community solar, but the mayor's office has committed to adding 1,000MW within the city by 2030. One project that neatly encapsulates the unique New York flavor of solar power is Sunset Park. Claimed to be the first New York City community solar project that's actually owned by a cooperative and not a nonprofit or government entity. Sunset Park allows people who own or rent homes (as well as small businesses) to access solar power without actually installing any solar equipment. Subscriber-members vote how the project invests its resources, so it's truly equitable.

Virgina ranks ninth on this list with 7,841 MW of capacity, but it only has 162 MWh of storage. This state's solar journey is shaped by the Virginia Clean Economy Act (VCEA), and its growth of solar capacity has been consistent. Nearly 10% of all power in the state comes from solar and its capacity is expected to more than double over the next five years.

This sounds like a tall order, but Virginia's track record here is impressive. The state had zero solar capacity in 2015, but by 2021, it was topping 3,500 MW. That represents massive coordination and investment at every level. The Virginia Clean Economy Act of 2020 played an important role here, and this act set a 16,100 MW capacity target with solar and wind combined. Virginia is about halfway there, but given how quickly these numbers have been growing, the timeline might be much shorter than the experts predict.

The Spotsylvania Solar project, is a remarkable example of how solar energy generation can be used not only to directly provide clean energy, but also to fund environmental protection. Combining four solar projects, Spotsylvania covers 6,350 acres of land. However, 2,000 acres of that are being preserved as undeveloped land for conservation purposes. That's in stark contrast to the land destruction involved when building coal or nuclear facilities, and it's one way Virginia is showing the way for green energy potential.

In order to get accurate rankings of current solar capacity of states, we used the most current rankings from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA). This is a national trade association for both the solar power generation industry and the renewable energy storage industry. It's a good place to find both official state data outlined in a clear way, and to see the various regional solar energy policies, and what policy changes SEIA is pushing for in each state.

Once we'd established the official rankings for each state from SEIA, we investigated federal and state sources of official information to see where that total solar capacity comes from and how it breaks down. Each of these states have been the most successful at building, growing, and managing their solar power industries, but they all have unique challenges, too.

Finally, we searched for notable or interesting solar projects on a state-by-state basis, that illustrate the renewable energy philosophy and creative problem solving of both government and private projects. With most states aiming for a 2050 carbon-free date, we expect all of these numbers to rise dramatically over the coming years, and solar energy to play a bigger and much more visible role in the daily lives of citizens all over the United States.

He stressed that EVs will play a key role in India’s goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047. “To achieve this, the Centre is strengthening the EV ecosystem through investments in charging infrastructure, battery manufacturing, research and skill development,” the minister said, urging consumers to shift to EVs to reduce dependence on imported petroleum. title: Healey wants 'swift action' on energy bill, but negotiators just getting started | WWLP
description:
Maura Healey talked to legislative energy affordability bill negotiators Thursday and sent them a letter on Friday urging “swift action” to resolve differences in House and Senate bills that are very different.
The governor’s office announced at 10:16 a.m. Friday that Healey would hold a press conference that afternoon, where her office distributed a letter she sent to the energy chairs and she talked about her energy affordability priorities.
Healey said she supports provisions to modernize procurement policies, accelerate new energy resource development and lower the cost of electricity.
“We’ve talked to them a lot over the last, well, several months,” Healey told reporters when asked whether she had talked to Cusack and Barrett about the letter.
The House passed its energy bill (H 5151) in February, proposing to cut the Mass Save program by $1 billion, and the Senate passed its own (S 3166) on July 1, proposing instead to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program.
text:
BOSTON (SHNS) – Gov. Maura Healey talked to legislative energy affordability bill negotiators Thursday and sent them a letter on Friday urging “swift action” to resolve differences in House and Senate bills that are very different.

Healey, who has spoken for more than a year about her energy agenda after filing a bill in May 2025, railed on utility companies during a State House press conference, two days after conferees tasked with hashing out the legislation met for the first time.

The governor’s office announced at 10:16 a.m. Friday that Healey would hold a press conference that afternoon, where her office distributed a letter she sent to the energy chairs and she talked about her energy affordability priorities.

“When it comes to utility companies, we’ve got to end business as usual. Utility companies are seeking rate hikes and excessive profits, while people and businesses are struggling to pay their bills,” Healey said, outlining the contents of her four-page letter to Rep. Mark Cusack and Sen. Mike Barrett.

Healey said she supports provisions to modernize procurement policies, accelerate new energy resource development and lower the cost of electricity. She said Friday that among a slate of other policies, she wants to change how utilities buy their energy, a “full audit” of utilities companies, and to end “sweetheart deals” that enable a profit bonus for being part of New England’s grid.

“We’ve talked to them a lot over the last, well, several months,” Healey told reporters when asked whether she had talked to Cusack and Barrett about the letter. “I talked to all of them as recently as yesterday. We’re going to keep talking because I think we all recognize how important it is that we get this done and that we take the actions that we can take to lower people’s energy bills.”

But Healey, who has taken heat from political opponents who say her energy policies are contributing to rising costs, isn’t the only one pitching lawmakers.

While Eversource supports an affordability focus and an all-of-the-above energy approach to address supply constraint issues, “At the same time, we must recognize that the lack of baseload supply causes the region to burn millions of gallons of oil during times of peak demand, adding billions in costs for customers across New England and significantly increasing carbon emissions to the environment,” Eversource spokesperson William Hinkle said.

“It is also important to note that increased investments in utility infrastructure will be necessary to support the commonwealth’s goals – such as bringing more solar online and strengthening demand response programs,” Hinkle continued.

The Mass Coalition for Sustainable Energy on Thursday wrote a letter to Cusack, Barrett, and other members of the committee urging them “to prioritize energy affordability” and “to refrain from adding new costs to already record-high energy bills.” The coalition’s letter opposed efforts to “create or expand incremental programs that will add costs,” sunset GSEP, “terminate the requirement that utilities must serve natural gas to customers that choose it,” and “‘securitize’ clean energy costs.”

“Should the product of this conference report fail to lower ratepayer bills or put the reliability and safety of our energy infrastructure at risk, we would urge conferees to table any energy legislation until next session,” the coalition, which includes some labor unions and business groups, wrote.

On the same afternoon that the governor was railing against utility companies, including a specific reference to Berkshire Gas, her Department of Public Utilities approved a settlement that would allow Berkshire Gas to increase its gas base distribution rates to generate approximately $18.5 million in additional revenues, down from the $28 million the company requested. The new rates are effective Saturday.

“The Department has considered the estimated bill impacts associated with the settled rate increase. The Department is mindful of the burdens associated with higher bills and recognizes that the magnitude of the proposed rate increase, even as reduced in the Settlement Agreement, is significant,” the DPU order said. “We also acknowledge that the Department must ensure that the rates we approve today are sufficient to ensure the financial viability of the Company, without which it cannot serve its customers. In doing so, the Department must balance the concerns of customers, the utilities who serve them, public officials, and other regulatory bodies, summed up in our goal of providing safe and reliable service at the lowest possible cost.”

National Grid Director of Strategic Communications for Corporate Affairs New England, Brendan Moss, said Friday that “Any final legislation should focus on measures that provide real, measurable affordability benefits for customers while preserving the investments necessary to maintain a safe and reliable energy system that drives our economy and maintaining customer choice. Approaches that simply shift costs to future customers, defer essential infrastructure work, remove customer choice, or repackage costs without reducing them will not deliver meaningful affordability.”

Massachusetts households pay some of the highest energy costs in the country, and lawmakers have pointed to billions of long-term savings that would come as the result of their energy proposals. The House passed its energy bill (H 5151) in February, proposing to cut the Mass Save program by $1 billion, and the Senate passed its own (S 3166) on July 1, proposing instead to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program.

Asked Friday which version of the bill she’d sign, Healey said, “Let’s see what I get, and let’s see how this process goes,” noting that she’s “concerned about utility profits when it comes to the GSEP program.” Healey also said that she thinks Mass Save is “something that should be reformed” and that she has called to “cap spending” on the program, but that “it’s a program that’s been around for a while. It’s played an important role.”

Cusack said on Wednesday that “there are a lot of agreements … and significant disagreements, as we know. And I look forward to working through those with some urgency to try to get relief to our constituents, the households, and businesses before this winter.”

Barrett added, “We should do this, ideally, before a November election, so that those of us who have races can point to an achievement.”

Asked what she makes of lawmakers pushing lawmaking past July 31 and into campaign season under new joint rules, Healey said, “I don’t think about it in terms of a campaign schedule.”

As to whether she has any indication of whether lawmakers are close to an agreement on energy, Healey said, “Well, they’re meeting. The good news is the conference committee met the other day. That was for the first time, and they’ve got, you know, a lot of work ahead.”

Healey was also asked about the potentially tumultuous nature of the relationship between energy chairs, and her strategy for getting them together and getting a bill to her desk before November. Healey replied: “I don’t accept any characterizations about members of the Legislature.” She did not stop to answer a question about whether she had spoken to House Speaker Ron Mariano or Senate President Karen Spilka on Friday, or if she planned to visit them.

title: China Doubles Down on Clean Energy Even as Coal Keeps Growing | OilPrice.com
description:
China has been rapidly growing its renewable energy portfolio for several decades to become the world leader in green energy.
However, despite its ambitious renewable energy plans, it also plans to continue expanding its coal production.
China is the largest energy consumer and greenhouse gas emitter in the world; however, it has also grown to become the biggest renewable energy producer globally.
Alongside renewable energy growth, China intends to continue supporting the expansion of the coal sector to ensure stability in its power sector.
In 2025, China contributed 78 per cent of global coal power capacity that commenced operations.
text:
China has announced plans to double down on its already ambitious renewable energy targets by massively expanding its solar and wind capacity by the end of the decade. China has been rapidly growing its renewable energy portfolio for several decades to become the world leader in green energy. However, despite its ambitious renewable energy plans, it also plans to continue expanding its coal production.

China is the largest energy consumer and greenhouse gas emitter in the world; however, it has also grown to become the biggest renewable energy producer globally. The government set an ambitious goal of reaching peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, despite its increasing power needs and its continual reliance on coal.

China installed around 360 GW of wind and solar power capacity in 2024 alone, which contributed over 50 per cent of global additions that year. This brought its total installed capacity to 1.4 TW, around one-third of the world’s 4.5 TW capacity. In addition to accelerating the rollout of solar and wind power, the government has also welcomed the adoption of cleantech and business models that support renewable energy growth, including battery storage, virtual power plants, and electric vehicles (EVs).

In July, China announced plans to increase solar and wind power production by 53 per cent by 2030, as part of the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan period. The plan was issued jointly by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration. China now aims to increase overall renewable energy production to 1.8 billion tons of coal equivalent (tce) by 2030 from 1.18 billion tce in 2025.

The government aims for wind and solar power, backed up by storage, to provide 8 per cent of their installed capacity during peak demand and supply 20 per cent of electricity use during demand spikes. It also plans to add over 300 GW of renewable energy that can be dispatched when demand spikes.

The plan plans to add 150 million tce of wind and solar use outside the power sector for sectors such as renewables-powered heating and cooling and green hydrogen, a sector whose production China aims to increase to 2 million metric tons by the end of the decade. The government also targets 570 GW of hydropower capacity, including 160 GW of pumped storage capacity, by 2030.

China currently has a solar power pipeline of around 664 GW planned or under construction, around one-third of the global total. The Asian giant also has almost 700 GW of proposed wind capacity, or one-quarter of the global total.

There are also plans to develop China’s deep-sea offshore wind bases and to integrate offshore wind with underwater data centres. Finally, China intends to pilot renewables megabases that transmit wholly renewable energy. Wind and solar power currently contribute around 20 per cent of the power China delivers through its ultra-high voltage transmission network, which moves power from megabases in the north and northwest to cities and factories in the east.

China aims to develop 10 megabases under its five-year plan 2026-2030 and has proposed 11 transmission lines delivering 129 GW of wind and solar power and 40 GW of coal power. The high proportion of coal generation in the power mix could potentially undermine the government’s clean energy aims. China could instead use energy storage technologies to make its intermittent renewables more reliable.

As part of the plan, the Chinese government also intends to continue expanding international cooperation on renewable energy, support the global green energy transition, and encourage the international adoption of its green energy technologies, standards, and certification systems.

Alongside renewable energy growth, China intends to continue supporting the expansion of the coal sector to ensure stability in its power sector. In 2025, China contributed 78 per cent of global coal power capacity that commenced operations. It is both the biggest consumer and the largest producer of coal worldwide, accounting for 86 per cent of the total global capacity under construction.

China’s coal power output increased in early 2026, which suggests its decrease in power-sector emissions in 2025 may have been temporary, even vis-à-vis record renewable energy growth. Power-sector emissions rose in the first four months of the year, although they remain below 2024 levels at present.

Qi Qin, an analyst at CREA, stated, “The situation is alarming… China has installed enormous amounts of solar and wind capacity, but the question is whether that capacity is being fully utilised.”

China is developing its renewable energy capacity at an extraordinary pace, faster than any other country. New targets suggest that China is rolling out wind and solar power even faster than it intended under its previous ambitious green energy targets. Nevertheless, its heavy dependence on coal and plans for further expansion have the potential to undermine its emissions reduction targets in the coming decades.

title: A nuclear New Deal in Italy - European Interest
description:
Italy is considering reactivating nuclear energy after a 4-decade absence following the Chornobyl nuclear disaster and multiple referendums on the topic.
To support this nuclear energy revival, the government hopes to gain support from younger generations.
Italy had two referendums on nuclear energy, but after nuclear disasters.
The first, in 1987, closed what was once one of Europe’s most advanced nuclear programmes due to fear after the Chornobyl nuclear disaster, the second, in 2012, in the wake of Fukushima’s fallout, only served to confirm Italians’ weariness of nuclear energy.
However, younger generations are less afraid of nuclear energy and less sceptical about its potential dangers.
text:
Italy is considering reactivating nuclear energy after a 4-decade absence following the Chornobyl nuclear disaster and multiple referendums on the topic.

Giorgia Meloni‘s government is spearheading a new energy policy that includes a soft reversal of the ban. Parliament is poised to approve legislation establishing a legal framework for next-generation nuclear technologies. This new government’s strategy centres on small modular reactors (SMRs) and advanced nuclear technologies.

Environment and Energy Security Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin described them as “much safer” and more suitable to Italy’s needs. These could begin operating between 2033 and 2035, addressing projected 30% increases in electricity demand while supporting climate goals.

To support this nuclear energy revival, the government hopes to gain support from younger generations.

Italy had two referendums on nuclear energy, but after nuclear disasters. The first, in 1987, closed what was once one of Europe’s most advanced nuclear programmes due to fear after the Chornobyl nuclear disaster, the second, in 2012, in the wake of Fukushima’s fallout, only served to confirm Italians’ weariness of nuclear energy.

However, younger generations are less afraid of nuclear energy and less sceptical about its potential dangers. A June 2026 survey reveals 55% of Italians support next-generation nuclear plants, with younger generations leading this shift. Unlike older Italians who remember Chornobyl as defining nuclear energy’s risks, younger Italians increasingly view atomic power through the lens of technological progress and climate solutions.

Despite this momentum, significant challenges remain. Critics question the economics, with estimates suggesting a single 300-megawatt SMR could cost between €3 and €6 billion. The political test ahead involves finding suitable locations for reactors and waste storage, as public support typically drops when local implementation is considered.

This article used information from The Associated Press.

A nationwide social movement is needed to speed up the adoption of renewable energy in Bangladesh, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, adviser to the prime minister on finance and planning, said on Saturday.
The discussion was organised by the Economic Reporters’ Forum in collaboration with the Distributed Renewable Energy Platform (DREP).
He said renewable energy could lower household energy costs, leaving families with more disposable income for other needs and investments.
He said the government has introduced fiscal incentives and policy reforms to encourage investment in renewable energy technologies and electric vehicle manufacturing.

text:
A nationwide social movement is needed to speed up the adoption of renewable energy in Bangladesh, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, adviser to the prime minister on finance and planning, said on Saturday.

He said public demand, rather than government policy alone, would drive the country’s transition to clean energy and reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels.

Speaking at a discussion titled “Distributed Renewable Energy: The Future Solar Solution for Bangladesh” at the Economic Reporters’ Forum (ERF) auditorium in Dhaka, Titumir said renewable energy should become a shared public cause to ensure a livable planet for future generations.

“Our first priority should be to build a social movement. We need collective and public action to make access to renewable energy a right,” he said.

The discussion was organised by the Economic Reporters’ Forum in collaboration with the Distributed Renewable Energy Platform (DREP).

Titumir said Bangladesh’s shift to renewable energy should start by creating public demand, arguing that the market will respond when people want cleaner energy.

“If we can create the demand, the supply system will follow,” he said, urging civil society organisations, NGOs and microfinance institutions to help expand access to distributed solar technologies.

He said renewable energy could lower household energy costs, leaving families with more disposable income for other needs and investments.

Highlighting Bangladesh’s reliance on imported fuels, Titumir said wider use of rooftop solar systems could significantly reduce gas and LPG consumption and improve the country’s energy security.

“Energy is sovereignty,” he said. “We must move away from the culture of dependence and build a culture of self-reliance.”

The adviser also stressed the need to develop local manufacturing of renewable energy equipment, including solar panels, batteries and inverters, to support the sector’s long-term growth.

He said the government has introduced fiscal incentives and policy reforms to encourage investment in renewable energy technologies and electric vehicle manufacturing.

Titumir also called on NGOs to include renewable energy financing in their microfinance programmes, saying development organisations could help speed up the adoption of clean energy across the country.

“The success of this transition depends on a social movement,” he said. “Every household, school, hospital, office and shop should gradually become part of the renewable energy journey.”

He added that expanding distributed renewable energy would reduce Bangladesh’s dependence on imported fuels, cut the import bill, strengthen energy security and support sustainable economic growth.

Others who spoke at the event included Khondaker Golam Moazzem, coordinator at DREP; Md Mehadi Hasan Shamim, research associate at CPD; ASM Munir, company secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association; Hasan Mehedi, chief executive officer of the Coastal Livelihood and Environmental Action Network; Ishtiaque Ahmed, director of engineering and innovation at SOLshare; Abul Azad, manager of Just Energy Transition at ActionAid Bangladesh; Doulot Akter Mala, president of the ERF; and Abul Kashem, the forum’s general secretary.

description:
A dam wall is not supposed to do anything except hold back water and get checked for cracks every few years.

Since the end of August 2022 it has also been a power plant.

text:
A dam wall is not supposed to do anything except hold back water and get checked for cracks every few years. The Muttsee dam in the Glarus Alps has been doing exactly that since 2016, sitting at 8,200 feet, higher than any other dam in Europe. Since the end of August 2022 it has also been a power plant.

There are 4,872 solar modules bolted to its south face, rated at 2.184 megawatts, running close to 3,000 feet along the wall. The interesting part is not that somebody built it. It is that a team from Switzerland’s EPFL spent a full year measuring what came out, then published the numbers.

From October 2022 to September 2023 the plant returned 1,434 kilowatt-hours per kilowatt of installed capacity. Of that, 43 percent landed in the winter half of the year, the stretch when Swiss solar normally goes quiet and the country starts importing power.

Meanwhile, the law Switzerland wrote to get dozens more high-altitude plants built has stopped taking applications. Of the 54 projects on the record, 26 are dead and none is finished.

The dam had already paid for the expensive part

Muttsee is the upper reservoir of the Limmern pumped-storage complex, which is why the site had a 16-kilovolt grid connection sitting there before anyone drew a solar panel on it. Axpo initiated the project and built it with Basel utility IWB, which holds 49 percent. Discount grocery chain Denner signed a 20-year power purchase agreement for the entire output.

The wall faces south and it is steep, which matters more than it sounds. Snow slides off a steep panel instead of sitting on it and turning the array into a very expensive white rectangle for four months.

Getting the hardware up there was the hard part. There is no road to the dam, so all 730 metric tons of steel, aluminum and glass went in by helicopter from the valley floor at Tierfehd over about four months. The lifting crane was taken apart down in the valley, flown up in pieces, and rebuilt on the crest.

The modules are Megasol glass-glass units in two sizes, 460 watts and 385 watts, pre-wired into tables 47 feet wide before they went on the wall. Frames are 1.6 inches thick, sized for snow load, and the design allows for drifts up to 16 feet.

The bottom 16 feet of wall was left bare on purpose, so the snow has somewhere to land.

Tilt is 51 degrees across most of the array and 65 degrees in places, against the 30 or so you would use down in a valley. Total cost was 8 million Swiss francs, roughly $10 million.

Christian Heierli, Axpo’s project manager on AlpinSolar, has since told the company’s own magazine that they did not pick the dam because it was cheap. They picked it because they knew it would get approved. The project drew no formal objections at all, which turned out to be a luxury nobody else in this story enjoyed.

A year of measurements, and 43 percent of it arrived in the cold half

The study came out of EPFL’s Laboratory of Cryospheric Sciences with ZHAW and the consultancy SUNWELL, and ran in Frontiers in Energy Research in June 2024. It measured the dam against a conventional 6-megawatt ground-mounted plant at Payerne, 1,476 feet up on the Swiss plateau and a fair stand-in for the national solar fleet.

Across the same 12 months, the dam produced 168 percent of what Payerne managed. Across the winter half, it produced 380 percent.

Winter here is a legal definition, not a vibe. Swiss energy law splits the year at October 1 and March 31, and that split is what the subsidy rules are written against.

The dam put 616 kWh/kWp into that window, 43 percent of its year. Payerne managed 26 percent of its own, smaller year. Capacity factor at Muttsee came in around 16 percent, performance ratio at 0.89, thermal capture losses at 0.3 percent, which is what happens when your power plant spends most of the year cold.

The authors flag one caveat themselves. This is a single year of data, and that particular January through May ran well below the multi-year average at the reference sites, which flatters the 380 percent figure.

The panels have two working faces and the wall wastes one of them

Here is the part that gets reported wrong nearly every time this plant comes up in English. The modules are bifacial, meaning both faces generate, and the standard explanation is that the back side harvests sunlight bouncing off the snow.

At Muttsee, it barely does. EPFL measured the annual optical bifacial gain at the dam at about 1.5 percent.

The reason is structural rather than optical. The modules hang roughly five feet off the concrete, and that gap exists so technicians can still walk the wall and map its cracks, which they are required to do at least every five years. Five feet of shaded concrete is not an albedo source.

What the dam actually runs on is altitude. It sits above the fog layer that parks over the Swiss plateau from October onward, the silicon stays cold, and the steep tilt meets a low winter sun almost head-on.

The snow-bounce effect is real, it just needs room to work. At EPFL’s open test rig near Davos, at a similar altitude, the same comparison came out at 19 percent for panels tilted at 60 degrees and 28 percent at 90 degrees. The best setup up there returned 1,853 kWh/kWp, well clear of the 1,434 the actual power plant delivered.

That gap is the study’s real finding, and it applies to every alpine project still on a drawing board. A test rig gets one perfect orientation. A full-size plant gets whatever the terrain allows, which at Muttsee means azimuths smeared from southeast to southwest, two tilt angles, and surrounding slopes throwing shade at inconvenient hours.

Some bottom-row modules also got buried in snow that first winter, costing an estimated 1 percent of annual output.

It is the same lesson coming out of every unconventional mounting scheme, from Austria’s vertical solar crosses at a glacier ski resort to the panels standing edge-on in a Bavarian lake. The physics works. The site decides how much of it you collect.

Muttsee would not qualify for the law it helped argue into existence

Switzerland passed its emergency solar package on September 30, 2022, six weeks after the dam went fully live. Known as the Solar Express, it stripped back permitting for large high-altitude plants and offered up to 60 percent of investment costs back as a one-off payment.

To collect, the Federal Office of Energy requires a plant to produce at least 10 gigawatt-hours a year and at least 500 kWh per installed kilowatt across the winter half. The scheme is capped at 2 terawatt-hours of new production nationwide.

Muttsee clears the winter test without breathing hard, at 616 kWh/kWp. It misses the other one by a mile. The plant was announced at 3.3 million kilowatt-hours a year, and Axpo’s own project page now describes it as producing around 3 million. Either figure is a third of the legal minimum.

So the flagship that spent two years being photographed as proof the concept works could not have collected a franc under the law it was built to argue for. It also predates that law, which makes the point twice.

Axpo was blunt about the economics from the start. Announcing the project in January 2021, CEO Christoph Brand said the missing regulatory framework meant “this type of plant is barely economically feasible”, and said the company was building it anyway to make a point.

The window has closed and nobody has finished a plant

Applications for the Solar Express shut on December 31, 2025. Parliament had already softened the test that March, dropping the requirement to be feeding power into the grid by that date and accepting a publicly filed building application instead. Projects that missed it are out.

An independent tracker run by Oberli Engineering, updated July 21, 2026, counts 54 projects. Twenty-six are finished in the sense that they are never happening: seven abandoned during preliminary study, three dropped later, and 14 voted down by the municipalities that would have hosted them.

Of the 28 still alive, exactly zero are complete. Four are partly built and generating. Add up everything either legally approved or already under construction and you get 78.2 megawatts and 115.6 gigawatt-hours a year, which is 5.8 percent of the 2 terawatt-hour target.

Canton Valais, where the idea was born and where the loudest projects were announced, had not built or legally approved a single plant by the end of 2025, according to an analysis by Swiss public broadcaster SRF published in January 2026.

Bern keeps adjusting the machinery. On November 26, 2025 the Federal Council dropped a proposed cap on Solar Express funding after 97 consultation responses came back against it, and swapped the old altitude bonus for a winter-power bonus on large plants commissioned from January 1, 2026.

A separate acceleration act took effect on April 1, 2026, handing cantons a single consolidated permitting procedure for solar and wind projects of national interest.

What the four working plants are reporting so far

Madrisa Solar, above Klosters at around 6,560 feet, ran roughly 3,600 modules through its first winter, about 20 percent of the finished plant, and produced about 1.5 gigawatt-hours between October and March. Output rose around 15 percent after the first snowfall. The full build is a 70 million franc project, about $87 million, with commissioning due by the end of 2027.

Sidenplangg in canton Uri has 13 percent of its array running and reports winter output roughly three times what valley plants managed. The operators declined to give the Keystone-SDA news agency any actual figures, which is its own kind of data point.

The dam, meanwhile, has picked up a second job. Since August 2025 it has been supplying tertiary balancing power to national grid operator Swissgrid under a pilot called PV4Balancing, throttling its output on command when there is too much electricity in the system. Pooled with other solar plants, it is now a grid asset rather than just a generator.

The uncomfortable summary is that the best-performing alpine solar plant Switzerland has measured is the one it built before the subsidy existed, on a wall somebody else had already poured, wired and inspected. Those walls are not being handed out. Neither, on the evidence of the last three years, are the permits.

title: Tidal Energy Could Cover 57% of US Electricity Demand, NREL Study Finds | OilPrice.com
description:
Tapping into the country’s tidal energy potential could be a major game changer for decarbonization and energy security in the United States.
Despite the country’s vast tidal energy potential, the United States currently has zero commercially operating tidal power plants.
Most tidal energy prototypes are large models affixed to the sea floor.
This testing site is small-scale and exploratory in nature, but could create valuable data for future tidal energy research and design.
And on the West Coast, a research institute in Menlo Park, California, is testing out underwater kites that could generate tidal energy for off-grid coastal communities.
text:
An Alaska-based tidal energy company is testing a new kind of small, modular turbine in the waters off of Massachusetts to try to take advantage of the United States’ vast and untapped tidal power potential. The turbine is being piloted in the strong tidal currents of Cape Cod to test the technology’s performance and durability in real-world conditions in order to explore whether it could be suitable for commercial scaling.

Tapping into the country’s tidal energy potential could be a major game changer for decarbonization and energy security in the United States. In 2021, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) found that the total energy potential of marine sources in the United States amounts to approximately 2,300 terrawatt hours per year, or 57 percent of the whole country’s electricity output in 2019. As such, “even if only a small portion of the technical resource potential is captured, marine energy technologies would make significant contributions to our nation’s energy needs,” the report found.

Despite the country’s vast tidal energy potential, the United States currently has zero commercially operating tidal power plants. The model currently being tested in the tidal canals of Cape Cod could therefore be an important first step toward tapping into this vast clean energy potential and bringing the technology one step closer to becoming a commercial reality.

Most tidal energy prototypes are large models affixed to the sea floor. The model being tested at the Marine Renewable Energy Collaborative’s (MRECo) Bourne Tidal Test Site (BTTS) is much smaller and modular, which could lend itself to simpler installation, scaling, and maintenance for potential commercial applications even in remote coastal communities. This testing site is small-scale and exploratory in nature, but could create valuable data for future tidal energy research and design.

“Our goal is to make marine energy easier to build, deploy, and maintain in remote areas,” Lance McMullan, Sitkana founder and CEO, was recently quoted by Interesting Engineering. “This testing is critical as we move toward commercial deployments,” McMullan went on to explain.

The location in the strong currents of Cape Cod, where water speeds can reach up to four knots, is ideal for pushing the system to its limits, providing essential insights into the module’s design. “BTTS is one of the few places where we can evaluate our entire system in one location,” McMullan told Offshore Energy. “Beyond measuring power performance, we’ll be able to observe operation in a real marine environment and better understand interactions with wildlife.”

The potential application and impact of this kind of technology extends far beyond the borders of the United States. While the United States and Canada boast the highest surveyed levels of wave energy potential, the technology could provide a significant amount of the world’s energy needs if fully exploited. A new report from Ocean Energy Europe concluded that ocean energy has the potential to supply 21 percent of the European Union’s current energy consumption and a whopping 13 percent of global electricity demand. This could be a complete game-changer for Europe as the continent struggles to establish energy independence and wean itself off of fossil fuel imports against the backdrop of seemingly endless energy crises.

Europe is currently leading in terms of spending on tidal energy research and development, but the United States is quickly catching up thanks to ‘substantial’ funding programs from the Department of Energy. The BTTS experiment is just one of many cutting-edge tidal technologies being explored in U.S. waters. In the Great Lakes, researchers from the University of Michigan have set up mini-prototype devices that could one day provide electricity to islanders in the region. And on the West Coast, a research institute in Menlo Park, California, is testing out underwater kites that could generate tidal energy for off-grid coastal communities.

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: Kansas loves clean wind energy. The Trump administration keeps blocking it | Opinion
description:
The federal meddling has prevented at least three Kansas wind farm projects — projects totaling 3,650 megawatts of affordable electricity — from coming onto the grid.
Throughout the country, the Department of Defense is holding up nearly 300 wind projects by failing to sign off on cursory agreements with the FAA.
In Kansas, wind energy has brought a lifeline to small towns and allowed local families to keep family farms unable to survive from corporate agribusiness monopolies and mechanization.
Registered Republicans have overwhelmingly benefited from clean energy investments in Kansas, yet the current administration employs underhanded tricks to keep Kansas out of the clean energy business.
According to polls, the Kansas public overwhelmingly wants clean energy.
text:
Millions of dollars of investment and jobs that should be moving forward are being kept from Kansas and Missouri by the Trump administration. The Pentagon is using Federal Aviation Administration red tape to keep businesses from investing in Kansas. The federal meddling has prevented at least three Kansas wind farm projects — projects totaling 3,650 megawatts of affordable electricity — from coming onto the grid.

Stalling these projects means no construction jobs, diversified farmer revenue, local taxes for Kansas communities or new electricity as demand surges.

Throughout the country, the Department of Defense is holding up nearly 300 wind projects by failing to sign off on cursory agreements with the FAA. On May 31, a number of regional renewable energy trade groups filed a lawsuit in federal district court. We need our representatives and local leaders to demand faster rulings to break this illegal logjam, especially with the tax credit deadline approaching.

The fact is that more than twice as many Kansans support building new wind farms in their local area as oppose it. There is even broader support for solar projects held up near airports, and hundreds of millions in low-income home efficiency dollars that the administration is also withholding without congressional authorization.

In Kansas, wind energy has brought a lifeline to small towns and allowed local families to keep family farms unable to survive from corporate agribusiness monopolies and mechanization. Registered Republicans have overwhelmingly benefited from clean energy investments in Kansas, yet the current administration employs underhanded tricks to keep Kansas out of the clean energy business.

Trump's attacks on rural investment that Kansas towns need are deeply unpopular and out of step with his party. The Pentagon has decided that it can unilaterally stop clean energy development on private lands, withholding revenue from farmers and other landowners who might rely on energy payments to keep their land and farms profitable.

According to polls, the Kansas public overwhelmingly wants clean energy. Wind power has invested $33 million in local communities and nearly $73 million in extra income to farmers and ranchers through energy lease payments. The clean energy industry has created nearly 10,000 jobs in Kansas, and there are nearly 5,000 megawatts of additional wind projects that are looking to be built in the state.

Our representatives need to protest this ridiculous de facto moratorium the Trump administration has placed to stop renewable energy investment in our region — and the benefits that come with it.

However, despite its ambitious renewable energy plans, it also plans to continue expanding its coal production.

text:
China has announced plans to double down on its already ambitious renewable energy targets by massively expanding its solar and wind capacity by the end of the decade. China has been rapidly growing its renewable energy portfolio for several decades to become the world leader in green energy. However, despite its ambitious renewable energy plans, it also plans to continue expanding its coal production.

China is the largest energy consumer and greenhouse gas emitter in the world; however, it has also grown to become the biggest renewable energy producer globally. The government set an ambitious goal of reaching peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, despite its increasing power needs and its continual reliance on coal.

China installed around 360 GW of wind and solar power capacity in 2024 alone, which contributed over 50 per cent of global additions that year. This brought its total installed capacity to 1.4 TW, around one-third of the world's 4.5 TW capacity. In addition to accelerating the rollout of solar and wind power, the government has also welcomed the adoption of cleantech and business models that support renewable energy growth, including battery storage, virtual power plants, and electric vehicles (EVs).

In July, China announced plans to increase solar and wind power production by 53 per cent by 2030, as part of the country's 15th Five-Year Plan period. The plan was issued jointly by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration. China now aims to increase overall renewable energy production to 1.8 billion tons of coal equivalent (tce) by 2030 from 1.18 billion tce in 2025.

The government aims for wind and solar power, backed up by storage, to provide 8 per cent of their installed capacity during peak demand and supply 20 per cent of electricity use during demand spikes. It also plans to add over 300 GW of renewable energy that can be dispatched when demand spikes.

The plan plans to add 150 million tce of wind and solar use outside the power sector for sectors such as renewables-powered heating and cooling and green hydrogen, a sector whose production China aims to increase to 2 million metric tons by the end of the decade. The government also targets 570 GW of hydropower capacity, including 160 GW of pumped storage capacity, by 2030.

China currently has a solar power pipeline of around 664 GW planned or under construction, around one-third of the global total. The Asian giant also has almost 700 GW of proposed wind capacity, or one-quarter of the global total.

There are also plans to develop China's deep-sea offshore wind bases and to integrate offshore wind with underwater data centres. Finally, China intends to pilot renewables megabases that transmit wholly renewable energy. Wind and solar power currently contribute around 20 per cent of the power China delivers through its ultra-high voltage transmission network, which moves power from megabases in the north and northwest to cities and factories in the east.

China aims to develop 10 megabases under its five-year plan 2026-2030 and has proposed 11 transmission lines delivering 129 GW of wind and solar power and 40 GW of coal power. The high proportion of coal generation in the power mix could potentially undermine the government's clean energy aims. China could instead use energy storage technologies to make its intermittent renewables more reliable.

As part of the plan, the Chinese government also intends to continue expanding international cooperation on renewable energy, support the global green energy transition, and encourage the international adoption of its green energy technologies, standards, and certification systems.

Alongside renewable energy growth, China intends to continue supporting the expansion of the coal sector to ensure stability in its power sector. In 2025, China contributed 78 per cent of global coal power capacity that commenced operations. It is both the biggest consumer and the largest producer of coal worldwide, accounting for 86 per cent of the total global capacity under construction.

China's coal power output increased in early 2026, which suggests its decrease in power-sector emissions in 2025 may have been temporary, even vis-à-vis record renewable energy growth. Power-sector emissions rose in the first four months of the year, although they remain below 2024 levels at present.

Qi Qin, an analyst at CREA, stated, "The situation is alarming… China has installed enormous amounts of solar and wind capacity, but the question is whether that capacity is being fully utilised."

China is developing its renewable energy capacity at an extraordinary pace, faster than any other country. New targets suggest that China is rolling out wind and solar power even faster than it intended under its previous ambitious green energy targets. Nevertheless, its heavy dependence on coal and plans for further expansion have the potential to undermine its emissions reduction targets in the coming decades.

By Felicity Bradstock for Oilprice.com

title: EV Battery Recycling: The Problem You Didn't Know Existed - CarBuzz
description:
The influx of aging EVs is inevitable, which makes EV battery recycling a critical issue we are largely unprepared to handle - at least right now.
EV Battery Decline And Battery Recycling Before a battery reaches a processing facility, it has to die - but that death is highly relative, because it is a slow, unavoidable chemical degradation.
